speechtext: In view of the fact that the government is now paying for any remedial action which has to be taken in these homes, I wonder if the minister can assure residents of Elliot Lake and elsewhere that the policy of paying for corrective action will continue to be followed by the government. speakeroldname: Hon. Alastair Gillespie (Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POSITION ON PAYMENT OF COST OF DEALING WITH HOMES CONTAMINATED BY RADIATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is an extremely complex and difficult question, as the hon. member will appreciate. He knows the situation in Elliot Lake. He knows that most of the houses which have been found to contain radiation above normal limits are houses which have been built not upon any waste fill but on ordinary rock. The radon concentration is a result, not of any act of man, but from the presence of radioactivity in the rock itself. The question then is: should the Government of Canada now assume responsibility for cleaning up a situation for which it had no responsibility in the first place?
The second point I wish to emphasize is this: we will not delay introducing the clean-up measures while we argue about whose responsibility it is. We have not done this in Port Hope and we will not do it in Elliot Lake. We will, of course, go to the companies in Elliot Lake, particularly those companies which own property, and we shall certainly say to them that we expect them to pay for the clean-up of their property.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought the hon. member was more of a gentleman; this does not seem to be the case. I simply ask him to refer to the premier of his own province and verify the facts as I have stated them. As the first item on the agenda, we discussed fiscal arrangements, and the essence of the proposal we put to the provinces bore on the problem of established programs of financing. I would add, before discussing that, that we covered a series of other subjects, notably the equalization payments, and our discussion consisted of putting before the provinces three options whereby these equalization payments would be continued by the federal government. The provinces agreed to choose one of those three options, and that is the way in which parliament would be asked to approve the continuation of these equalization schemes.
The more difficult problem concerned the financing of established programs. The essence of these proposals was to provide, since they were successful, one joint step toward decentralization in Canada. I am talking of fiscal decentralization, not administrative decentralization. I have had occasion to discuss this program, of which the House is aware, in other forums and at other times following, particularly, the first ministers' conference last spring. At that time, I believe it was in June, I put a proposal before parliament and the first ministers. In essence, point one of that proposal is that it will provide more money to the provinces than if we were to continue the present schemes as they concern hospitalization, medicare and post-secondary education.
I have some simple figures on that, Mr. Speaker. It would suffice if I said that in 1977-78, as a result of this established program financing proposal, the provinces next year will receive some $221.2 million more than if we were to continue with the present schemes. By the year 1981 they will be receiving more than $1 billion more annually, and of course the figure will continue to grow. During the negotiations we added another two tax points to the federal offer, plus a levelling of payments, with the result that next year the provinces will get some $460 million more than had been the case before we began these discussions yesterday. When I say
Federal-Provincial Conference
that there is more money for the provinces than they would get under the existing arrangements, I mean that next year they will get, as a start, some $681 million more than under the present arrangements. This amount, if it is projected five years to 1981, will be to the extent of $ 1,718 million a year.
I do not add to this sum $130 million that the Minister of National Health and Welfare has also offered them under extended health care proposals. The provinces have asked for some more weeks to consider whether they will accept that or not. However, they have all accepted these established program financing schemes. I repeat, the effect of it will be some $681 million more next year to the provinces.
The advantage of this scheme is that there will be greater equality between the provinces due to the fact that up until now shared cost programs meant that the federal government was giving 50 cent dollars to the provinces. After they spent 50 cents to get our 50 cents, they were permitted to do certain things in the areas of hospitalization, medicare, post-secondary education, and so on. The advantage of these programs is that even the less wealthy provinces, which sometimes could not match this 50 cents with the federal government, will now receive the money regardless of what they themselves spend.

They will receive it on a per capita basis, regardless of what they spend. Half of it will be paid by way of tax points. This will total some 13'A tax points which the provinces will now be able to levy, painlessly, if I can describe it that way, by the fact that we will make that room by withdrawing to that extent from the present tax field. These tax points will be equalized to the average value in Canada as the equalization calculations are made.
The other half will be paid in cash on a per capita basis. This tax allowance will grow year after year on a three-year moving average based on gross national expenditure. It will also be equalized so that all provinces receive the same amount per capita, regardless, once again, of their tax base and particular wealth. These arrangements also provide greater flexibility to the provinces in the use of their own funds. There will only be very general conditions attached to the payment of these funds. The House knows the type and conditions to which I allude. For example, in medicare it will be the general conditions of transportability, universality, and so on.
The provinces will no longer have to submit their accounting to the federal government, or submit to a detailed set of rules as they have been up until now under, for example, hospitalization insurance. This will also mean there will be greater stability in the arrangements, since the provinces will be receiving fixed and known tax points and variable cash amounts but predictable based on the moving gross national expenditure. Therefore, the provinces and the federal government will have a much greater budgeting predictability. I might add that because we will no longer have to ask for detailed audit records from the provinces on how they spent

That is the essence of the established program of financing schemes. It will have the great advantage of us now being allowed to bring before parliament a system of assisting the provinces in the health area and in the area of post-secondary education. The system which will have all of these advantages will permit us to go to this scheme even in the area of hospital insurance. speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext:
I believe I have covered the main aspects of this discussion of the past few days. There are a great number of details and I will not burden the House with them. I will gladly answer questions on the various subjects that might interest the opposition parties. If that is a good enough base for the opposition to ask questions, I will merely sum up the conference to repeat that we have taken a giant step forward in decentralizing fiscal arrangements in Canada, an arrangement which is consistent with the repeated expression of the wish by the provinces to have greater autonomy in the administration of their programs and greater room in which to levy their own taxes.
This is a further step forward in the application of the belief that both the federal government and the provinces should be free to tax to fulfil their own needs. We are departing from previous regimes where the federal government was doing most of the taxing and the provinces were receiving the money to spend. We are returning ever more closely to the principles of fiscal responsibility whereby the taxing authority is also the spending authority. By transferring to the provinces these 13 Vi tax points, there will be a great transfer of the taxing authority to the provinces. We believe this is consistent not only with the wish of the provinces but in the direction in which the federal government has been going in the past several years.
I would merely add that there is a limit to the rule that can be followed in this regard. That limit is due, of course, to the fact that all provinces and all regions in Canada are not equally wealthy. As long as we are the government, we will consider it our duty to retain a sufficiently large section of the tax field so that we can make equalization payments to the provinces and transfer funds, as it were, from the richer to the poorer regions of Canada. In order to do this, of course, we must keep sufficient tax room for the federal government.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while 1 have not had an opportunity to analyse all the fiscal details just revealed to the House by the Prime Minister, to determine whether or not they will benefit or be detrimental to the provinces or to the

federal government, and while I particularly noted the omission from his remarks of any reference to the revenue guarantee, it is the process by which these decisions were arrived at, and not the particulars, to which I wish to make reference. The Prime Minister's statement has revealed, once again, that given the will and the determination, Canadian federalism works.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext:
The machinery may be creaky, the process may involve considerable tension and frustration, the eventual settlements may leave none of the partners fully satisfied; but federalism does produce something all the partners can live with until the next round of negotiations. To paraphrase Churchill's well-known remark about democracy, it is the worst of systems except for all possible alternatives.
The latest round of negotiations has shown a recognition of this essential fact on the part of both the provincial and the federal governments. The provinces were the first to recognize the necessity of accommodation. For the first time, they were able to reconcile their diverse particular goals-initial goals ranging from Ontario's desire for the transfer of 20 tax points to the desire of some of the less wealthy provinces to maintain an all-cash payments system-into a common provincial position they could all support.
The federal government was slow to respond to this example of accommodation and at various times in the past month, even as late as yesterday afternoon, it appeared to be taking a position that the maintenance of confederation was not worth a single tax point. The Minister of Finance earlier this month, and the Prime Minister yesterday afternoon, seemed prepared to call into question the effectiveness of our federal system in order to achieve a $215 million saving-the value of a single tax point-in compensation to the provinces in lieu of the revenue guarantee.
I am pleased the federal government has pulled back from the brink of such folly. I welcome its last-minute recognition that accommodation is the essence of the process in which we are engaged. The rigidity which the Prime Minister has displayed in the past has been extremely dangerous to the concept of federalism. I trust that while defending the legitimate interests of the national government, he and his colleagues will act on the basis of acceptance of the reality of Canadian federalism in the future.
But while the abandonment of folly is the cause for relief, it is no ground for congratulation. I say this because the government came very close, dangerously close, to handing the new government of Quebec exhibit A in the case it is amassing against federalism. The federal government was set on a course which would have enabled the advocates of separatism to say that our system of federal-provincial accommodation was bankrupt, that its inevitable products were deadlock and confrontation, and that the interests of the various levels of government could never be reconciled as part of national solutions acceptable both to the individual partners and to the nation.
December 14, 1976

All of us who sit in this House know how false a picture that is of the reality of Canadian federalism. We appreciate that the tension of honest disagreement may be a creative force as well as a frustrating obstacle to consensus. Equally, we all appreciate, I hope, that the government of Quebec will take every opportunity to add substance to its own particular analysis of our federal system. These people want to show that the break-up of that system is already a fact-that they have simply been the first to recognize that reality, and that the division of the country is the logical and inevitable next step.
It is vital that all of us in Canadian political life lay new emphasis on the fact that our system, despite its imperfections, does work. It is incumbent on all those in positions of power who share this view to see to it that the system is seen to be working. Once again, we have seen that system work. But in the process, the reluctance, the hesitation of the federal gover-nemnt to recognize its legitimate role added needless strains to federalism and raised doubts about its viability. I commend those responsible at the federal level for finally playing the role which they are duty-bound to play. I am concerned that they took so long to grasp their duty.
In the drama of conflicting goals which is a necessary reality of federal-provincial negotiations, it is only too easy for players and spectators to lose sight of the fact that the essence of the game is not to achieve victories for one side at the expense of the other but to reach a viable accommodation through which both levels can pool their powers and resources to benefit the people they ultimately represent. Between them, the federal and provincial governments have all the legislative power necessary to undertake any task they can agree upon. Federalism is the process through which they maximize their capacity to serve our people. This is too vital a responsibility to pursue frivolously or in an adversary spirit. That is obvious common sense. Now, more then ever, is the time to preach that common sense, in word and in deed. May we have more such preaching by example?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure the House appreciates the Prime Minister coming from a very exhausting conference and making a statement in the House today regarding the proceedings of that conference.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext:
It is unfortunate that it was not possible for us to get a copy of the statement he was going to make, but I can quite understand that this would not have been practicable because of the shortness of time. I am sure members will have ample opportunity to ask the Prime Minister questions, and I hope the right hon. gentleman will table documents giving full details of the fiscal arrangements which have been made between the federal government and the governments of the respective provinces.
The Prime Minister divided the agenda of the conference into two parts. First, he dealt with the area of economics and began, with becoming modesty, by saying that all the prov-
Federal-Provincial Conference
inces were agreed as to the success of the controls which were imposed by the government a year ago last October. He did not add, of course, that some of the provinces have already announced that they do not intend to renew their agreement with respect to the controls. So it would appear that their conviction as to the value of the controls did not go very far. The Prime Minster said he hoped this would convince the opposition parties of the value of these controls. I want to say that as far as this party is concerned, we have never objected to an incomes policy. What we objected to was an incomes policy which was weighted almost entirely against people who work for wages and salaries, while allowing the corporate and professional groups to get off comparatively scot-free. That situation has not been rectified, and until it has we will continue to oppose a system that is both unjust and inequitable.
I was surprised that the Prime Minister said nothing about what I would have thought would have been two very important matters at a federal-provincial conference. The first is unemployment. Was that not discussed? Did the federal government not put forward any plans? Did it tell the provincial premiers what it was going to do about Work Canada and what kind of program the government will undertake this winter to put unemployed people to work? Was that passed by as a relatively unimportant subject?
Were there no discussions with respect to energy? This country, whether it knows it or not, is heading for a precipice when it comes to energy supply. The provinces, particularly those provinces that produce the energy resources, have a very just complaint about how they have been dealt with by the federal government. Were no steps taken at the conference to resolve the problems of the energy producing provinces and to work out a fair accommodation between them and the federal treasury? Nothing was said about that. It would be very interesting for us to find that out during the next few weeks.
The second part of the Prime Minister's statement had to do with fiscal arrangements. He made no mention of the revenue guarantee provisions which have been giving a good deal of concern to the provinces. I hope we will get some further elucidation on that matter, if not from the Prime Minister, at least from the Minister of Finance. With reference to an equalization formula, the Prime Minister said that three options had been placed before the provinces. It would have been useful if the Prime Minister had told us what the three options were, but I am sure he will do that in answer to any questions which are asked following the statements by the various parties.
The Prime Minister said that one of the steps taken at the conference was to introduce a greater measure of financial decentralization. There is a considerable amount of merit in financial decentralization, just as there ought to be a good deal of merit in flexibility in a federal system with respect to preserving the culture, traditions and languages of the founding races of this country. One of the reasons fiscal decentrali-

Federal-Provincial Conference
ration is necessary is that under the agreements entered into- and they were very good agreements in the main-the provinces were paid a percentage of a stipulated sum of money for a specific purpose. Sometimes that money was paid for a service which was already adequate but the province could not spend the money on some other service which was inadequate. Therefore, the idea of flexibility is something that is necessary and which we support.
The danger, Mr. Speaker, is that when we introduce flexibility and fiscal decentralization, we must not lose sight of two basic principles: the first is that the provinces must be assured of sufficient revenue to discharge the responsibilities which have been allocated to them. That is why, for instance, we objected so strenuously to the government's proposal that the contributions to medical and hospital insurance and postsecondary education should be tied to the gross national product, because there is no relationship whatever. In 1975 the gross national product rose less than 1 per cent, but the cost of providing health services rose by 16 per cent. How could the provinces discharge their responsibilities in a situation like that? The other rigid principle which must be adhered to in any financial decentralization is to see to it that the principle of making available to every citizen of Canada, irrespective of where he or she may live, an equal standard of services is applied. I am still not satisfied from the statement we have had from the Prime Minister that these aims are going to be fulfilled.
The Prime Minister said the government is going to give the provinces some 13'/2 percentage points, but it is only going to equalize those to the average for Canada. I think the provinces have been asking for a long time, quite justly, that it should be equalized to the two top provinces. I think that would be much fairer. The danger with tax points is that if revenue drops drastically, the federal government has other sources of revenue on which it can call to meet the situation, but the provinces that depend on these tax points will still have to provide services even though their revenues are either standing still or declining. So I think we can say of this conference that every member of this House, irrespective of party, hopes that its outcome will mean a strengthening of the bonds of confederation.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext:
We want to hold this country together, but it is not going to be held together by rhetoric, by confrontation or by debate between the head of the Canadian government and the heads of provincial governments. In the main, Canada will be held together if the people in the respective provinces feel that they are getting fair and just treatment and that there is equality of treatment for all sections of this country.
I want to remind the House that we have moved a long way since the report of the Rowell-Sirois commission. That was the first charter of provincial rights and services for the people of Canada which was written in this country. That commission, which sat for several years in this city and produced what I

think is a monumental report, laid down principles which I urge the government and the House, as well as the provincial governments, not to forget, namely, that every Canadian, no matter where he or she lives, no matter their race, colour or religion, should be entitled to the same level of services with respect to health and education and their general welfare.
I submit that we should examine the proposals which are coming out of this conference in light of that basic principle laid down by the Rowell-Sirois commission. Because if we are not able to adhere to those principles, then instead of having strengthened confederation we will have weakened it.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I thank the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) for coming in this House and giving the results of that important federal-provincial conference. I think that the first step was made, as the Prime Minister just said, towards the good understanding that the federal government wishes to establish with the provinces.
However there is a question I ask myself: If the Bourassa government had maintained itself in power in Quebec I do not know if the Prime Minister would have been so open at that first ministers' conference. I think the province of Quebec gave itself the tools needed to open a door that had to be opened. Also, I think that the Prime Minister said in his statement that from now on, and particularly from 1980, the provinces would have more taxation powers.
I think it was the wish of the Fathers of Confederation and that tax equalization, that is taxation power, should be for the most part in the hands of the provinces and that the federal government should be more favourable to it. I congratulate the Prime Minister for having said that the door should be opened "slowly". I believe the Prime Minister is right to say that, as there are poor and rich provinces. I think it would be absolutely wrong and even harmful for the federal government to open its purse too easily as it would create a precedent and would not prevent some provinces from using it to dismember Canada.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to put a question to the Prime Minister. He made reference in his remarks to the hospital insurance plan and the agreement to have participation start on April 1. I wonder if the Prime Minister could tell us whether the agreement to that starting date was a condition required from the provinces before the government of Canada would agree to the transfer of the two tax points referred to?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: Yes, in part, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext:
This is really another question, Mr. Speaker. I wonder whether the Prime Minister would like to take the opportunity to correct an impression I think he left on the record in his earlier remarks when he suggested there would be a net gain to the provinces of some $630 million as a result of this arrangement, when in fact what happens is that the

provinces will be receiving in the neighbourhood of some $270 million less next year than they would have had the existing arrangements remained in effect. I wonder if the Prime Minister would like to take the opportunity of correcting that misimpression he left on the record?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. I can say unequivocally that the Leader of the Opposition is wrong.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, we can say unequivocally that the Prime Minister and I disagree, and I certainly am prepared to carry the case both in and beyond this chamber. It is our understanding that the question of constitutional matters was delayed to a later point on the agenda, to be reached if possible. I wonder whether the Prime Minister could tell us if there were discussions of plans relating either to the content or possible patriation, or the nature of an amending formula relating to the constitution and, if so, what was the nature of those discussions? subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did canvass the premiers informally on the subject. It was not on the agenda, as the House knows. I got from them what I believe to be a consensus that in this area they would want to make haste slowly, and apparently not take any immediate initiative in this regard. For that reason I did not propose a date to them for a federal-provincial conference on the constitution. I will be having further contact with the chairman of the provincial premiers, Premier Lougheed, about the possibility some time in the new year of looking at a date.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: One last question, Mr. Speaker. Is it, then, the position of the government of Canada that it will not be moving unilaterally on any matters relating to the constitution?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: I did not say that, Mr. Speaker. I indicated that if we were going to have a federal-provincial conference, the dates would be discussed with the first ministers. I would certainly want to do one thing, and perhaps this means moving unilaterally in a very restricted sense: I would want to put on the record an answer to Premier Lougheed's letter of last October.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Prime Minister in respect of the agreement on the two tax points in place of a revenue guarantee, and the particular apprehension that was shared by some of the poorer provinces in respect of the federal proposals. I believe there were some studies done concerning the impact that these new fiscal arrangements would have, particularly on the five eastern provinces.
I wonder whether the Prime Minister would indicate if there will be any direct shortfall to these provinces, whether the Department of Regional Economic Expansion will be expected
Federal-Provincial Conference
to enter into new arrangements to offset any economic difficulty and, in particular, whether the two tax points were considered effective in respect of these provinces when additional tax points are usually not beneficial in terms of provincial tax revenues?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the last part of the question, or remarks, I would indicate that the two tax points are to be paid, one by way of a tax point which will be equalized to the national average, and the other half-or the other tax point, as it were-will be paid in cash. These cash payments will be the equivalent, at the outset, of one tax point and will vary from year to year in the way indicated earlier.
On the general subject of revenue guarantee, Mr. Speaker, I did not touch upon it in my opening statement for the very simple reason that we have always stated in this House and outside that this revenue guarantee was for a period of five years. The provinces hoped that this guarantee program for five years would be prolonged, and it was in that sense that they were asking for four tax points. There had never been any commitment or indication that we would give that, but naturally the provinces were trying to get it. We took the view that the revenue guarantee was finished, as we have said it would be. The provinces had five years to adapt to the tax reform, and now under our system they are free to modify their taxes and increase rates as they will.
The two points that we put on the table and which the provinces accepted can be considered by them, if they wish, as a final phasing out of the revenue guarantee. We did not put it forward in that spirit, Mr. Speaker. It was a way of enriching, at least in part, the established program of financing sufficiently so that they would have no hesitation in coming into the scheme, because they would be so much better off, as I have indicated by the figures, by coming in under the scheme than by not doing so.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has not totally answered my question in respect of the economic situation of the poorer provinces. Perhaps he might answer that, in addition to answering clearly whether, as a result of the settlement on these two tax points, which the Prime Minister suggested may or may not be regarded as being in place of a revenue guarantee, particularly in view of the expression of opinion by some premiers following the conference that they were still considerably short in terms of their revenue expectations from the federal government, there will be further negotiations regarding the revenue shortfall from that under the revenue guarantee which the federal government is now discontinuing?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot agree with the premise of the question as stated regarding a shortfall. I repeat, the result of this conference is that the provinces, including the five easternmost ones the hon. member mentioned, are in a substantially better position than they were before. Just to refer to the established program of financing, in the case of one province, because of this program, it goes away with $40 million more next year and in five years this will be $188

December 14, 1976
Federal-Provincial Conference
million. That is in respect of Quebec. So there is no shortfall; it is benefiting from this change.
In so far as the two points are concerned, and once again to take the largest of the five easternmost provinces, it gets $ 117 million more because of these two tax points and the levelling provision. So the total in the case of that province is $160 million, at the end of a day and a half of conference, over what it had when it went into the conference. So there is no question of shortfall.
The hon. member asked questions about DREE. Of course DREE will continue to operate in the provinces of Canada under its mandate, but this will be regardless of the results of this conference. This was not a subject which was discussed. The provinces come out of this better off than before, but we still feel that there is ample room for the operations of DREE.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 wish to put a question to the Prime Minister. Granted that the government is trying to maintain a balance between fiscal decentralization and the responsibility of the federal government to maintain equal standards across the country, may I ask if there have been any studies or projections as to what will happen to the levels of health and education in the various provinces under these new arrangements? When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) is answering that question, I wonder if he would answer this one also: Is the federal government prepared, or does it stand committed, to come back into the picture if it is necessary to maintain equal standards across Canada in the fields of health and education?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext:
This is a very intricate question, and I will attempt to do justice to it as simply as possible. The very title of the program, Established Programs Financing, indicates that in mature schemes like hospital insurance, post-secondary education and medicare, we are in a sense gambling that the provinces will want to continue to be deeply involved and that they will not go back on the high standards of service which have been established over the past decade and a half in Canada in those three areas. They are established programs. They were started with shared-cost programs. We now feel that they are sufficiently established that the provinces can be trusted, as it were, to continue putting a lot of their own money into these programs, and that is why our payments by way of tax points and of cash grants lets them float free, as it were, and administer these programs without detailed federal overseeing. So there is a trust in the provinces that they will act in the way in which the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre hopes; and we share that hope.
In so far as whether we can at some stage down the road correct a deteriorating situation, if such should develop the answer is yes, in part. The hon. member will realize that we tranferred tax points and cash grants. The hon. member will realize, also, that the programs are for five years, but they can be, I think, terminated with a three-year notice provided the three-year notice is not given before two years from now; that

is a more correct way of saying it. But these programs can come to an end, at which point, if some provinces are not doing their share and are just using the federal share in order to fund post-secondary education, and so on, we might want to review the situation. I say this not by way of threat but to indicate that the parliament of Canada will certainly want to look down the road some distance at whether the federal funds which are given to the provinces for these three programs are spent in a way which shows good will on the part of the provinces. That will be for the House to judge.
I repeat that there is no detailed accounting required, but the provinces will be obliged, in the area of medicare and in the other areas, to follow certain broad conditions. I mentioned affordability, universality, and so on, so that the programs can come to an end. They are not for ever. But, of course, if they are, it will mean that we would want to review our paying of cash in so far as the tax room which we have granted is concerned. Of course, there is no way in which we can get that back from the provinces. They will occupy that tax room, and that is forever in the sense that if we want to get back into that tax room we cannot do it painlessly by expecting them to withdraw as we have withdrawn today.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: I do not want to make too much of the word "gambling", which the Prime Minister used; I realize he just used it off the cuff. But when there is talk about gambling with health and education, some of us get a bit concerned. However, is it clear that if the provinces are not able to maintain equal standards of medicare, hospitalization and education across the country the federal government will recognize its responsibility and its commitment to see that those standards are maintained for all Canadians, wherever they live?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: I will give a very short answer. Perhaps the situation the hon. member envisages a few years down the road is correct. Perhaps it is not a gamble because we do not think the provinces will behave in the way the hypothesis of the hon. member suggests, but if somewhere down the road it appears that the provinces are not satisfying the hon. member's conception of what they should be doing-

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: Or if they are not able to do so.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: Or indeed, if they are unable to, the program can come to an end. We do not see it as being terminated by the federal government, but there is provision that with two years' notice it could come to an end, and arrangements which the hon. member might explore and find more equitable could be studied.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, given the outcome of this first ministers' conference and the concessions made to the provinces by the federal government, would the Prime Minister tell the House whether Quebec Premier Rene Levesque seemed enthusiastic about or at least satisfied with the result of this conference?
December 14, 1976

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I suggest it would be a euphemism to say that the Quebec premier had not in mind to depict federalism in a most constructive and effective light. subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, considering his mood throughout the conference, before leaving could the Prime Minister tell the House whether he tried to come to an agreement with one or two provinces or a province in particular, and I am referring here to Alberta, either to place a veto or submit another formula to frustrate that conference?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: I do not know whether I understand the question but surely the federal government did not want the conference to fail and I do not think that the provinces had an understanding to that end. Prime Minister if there is talk of reevaluating the basic fundamentals of federalism and, considering the importance of achieving and maintaining this national unity, if the Prime Minister intends honoring the wishes of the provinces and going ahead with a basic reevaluation of all aspects of our federalism by means of a federal-provincial conference?

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, I must state from the start that I do not concur with the views of the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle) when he states that the current situation is that of Quebec versus the federal government. Unless I am mistaken, the members on this side of the House who were elected by Quebec residents maintain they represent that province in the same way as do the members elected to the provincial legislature. Then it was a question of provincial governments and the federal government striving to achieve, each at its own level, the maximum benefits for the Canadian population. The hon. member's proposal is very vague and very general. If he could be more specific, I could try to answer him. But, Mr. Speaker, I can only answer in the negative for the time being when he speaks of a general conference to reevaluate our Confederation.
We all know very well that the Quebec premier is saying right and left that his main purpose is to separate his province from the rest of the country, and achieve independence. Whereas I take for granted that it is not in the best interests of his government to try to revamp the Confederation as we know it now, if such an operation did not result in the separation of his province and it is a subject I do not wish to discuss with him for the moment.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, first of all I want to congratulate the right hon. Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet who accompanied him for the tremendous success of this conference. subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will try my best to be as gentlemanly as I am capable of being.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: The Prime Minister raised some doubts as to this. The Globe and Mail calls me "courtly"; surely the Prime Minister can do better than that.

Canadian Tax Foundation in Vancouver a couple of weeks ago? Is there any assurance that Canada has a place, which it has not had up to now, and surely must have in post-secondary education, more than just a money place?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the situation about which the Prime Minister has been speaking is a very complicated one, but if I understood him correctly he said that the provinces were going to receive $460 million more than when the discussions first began-presumably that is in connection with the revenue guarantee-and they would receive $231 million more next year in established program financing in shared-cost programs, or $681 million more than under the present arrangements; but at the same time they will lose $900 million which they received this year in revenue guarantee. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate the Prime Minister, his colleagues and all provincial representatives-

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext: -for having concluded an agreement, apparently, of course, with some stick-handling on both sides. If these negotiations and arrangements are such a great deal for the provinces as the Prime Minister said, I should like to ask him what the real fiscal advantages, the administrative advantages and disadvantages are to the federal government and to the public generally, on a national basis.

subtopic: FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL RELATIONS FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE-REPORT THEREON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in so far as the federal government is concerned, there are advantages. One will be greater predictability in our own budgeting. As the hon. member knows, in the past, under the shared-cost programs, we did not have much choice. It was open-ended in the sense that if some province decided to spend a great deal of money on hospitalization, we had to match that with 50-cent dollars and, therefore, could not predict from province to province what they would want to spend.
Budgeting will be much more certain now that tax points will have been transferred and the value of the money will be known from year to year based on a three-year escalating average. So there is greater certainty and much greater accounting simplicity from both the point of view of the provinces and the federal government. We will no longer have to enter upon detailed audits of the books of hospitals, school systems, university systems, the medical profession, and so on. It will be much simpler to operate. As a general advantage to the people of Canada, I would say it is a step toward a principle which I believe is recognized in our democracy, that as far as possible the government which spends should also be the government which taxes. This is a joint step in that direction.

subtopic: CONSTITUENCY RECORDS ACT

speechtext: The House resumed, from Wednesday, December 8, consideration of the motion of Mr. Allmand that Bill C-9, to approve, give effect to and declare valid certain agreements between the Grand Council of the Crees (of Quebec), the Northern Quebec Inuit Association, the Government of Quebec, la Societe d'energie de la Baie James, la Societe de developpement de la Baie James, la Commission hydro-electri-que de Quebec and the Government of Canada and certain other related agreements to which the Government of Canada is a party, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.

speakeroldname: Mr. Joe Clark (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity for taking part in this debate on a bill which has been of great concern for some time to the House of Commons and on a process which has been of great concern to us all. I might be pardoned if I digress for a moment to draw to the attention of the House the fact that in the last few moments the hon. member for Lanark-Renfrew-Carleton (Mr. Dick) introduced more legislation into the House of Commons than the government has introduced in the first months of this session.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext:
I want to deal in a serious manner with Bill C-9. I believe that this legislation and the process which brought this legislation to the House of Commons is an example for us all to note and, in the future, for us all to avoid, in that it amounts to a shameful betrayal of trust and responsibility by the government of Canada for native peoples who are under the jurisdiction of the government of Canada. I want to begin, sir, by reviewing for members of the House of Commons the history of the James Bay agreement, an agreement to which this legislation would give effect. That history began in April, 1971.

When former Quebec premier Bourassa made a statement on a hydro electric development in the James Bay area, he did so for political reasons. There had been no consultations, no study on its impact on the environment, the Indian population or other people living in the area. Nor were there any negotia-
December 14, 1976

tions up to the time when the Indians instituted legal proceedings before the courts of the province of Quebec.

As all of us know, the Cree people of the James Bay region won an injunction in November, 1973, in a court in Quebec. That injunction was suspended weeks later by the Court of Appeals of that province, and the Supreme Court of Canada refused the Council of Cree leave to appeal in the Supreme Court in December, 1973. As a consequence of that, as members who followed the matter will remember, the native people were forced to negotiate the manner of their response to the James Bay project which had been forced upon them by a political decision of the government of Quebec.
I should draw to the attention of the House, for emphasis and to refresh memories which might have faded in the intervening two years, that the native people of James Bay, people whose lives were spent, by and large, in an atmosphere distant from the metropolitan centres of Canada, were forced to negotiate under circumstances that were very difficult to all of them. The negotiations did not occur on their land. The negotiations about their land did not occur on their land and did not occur in circumstances or an environment with which they were familiar. Instead, the native peoples were hauled down to Montreal and forced to deal, they being people accustomed to a very different way of life, with the accumulated might of Crown corporations, the government of Quebec and other agencies. This might was brought to bear against them and against their hereditary practices and dealt with the future of that land which had been traditionally theirs in the James Bay region. The negotiations into which they were forced to enter did not occur where they were comfortable. They occurred, instead, in downtown Montreal. It is important for all of us to recognize that these negotiations occurred under the gun of a general deadline.
It was clear from the outset that it was necessary for the native people concerned in the James Bay region to come to an agreement by November 1, 1975, and it was clear from the outset, certainly to them, that if they did not come to an agreement by that time a settlement would be imposed upon them. Indeed, so rigid was this government which had the responsibility to protect these people, so rigid was it in the imposition of that deadline, that it refused even the simple request for the deadline to be extended by a month, a matter of 30 days, when we drew near to the November 1 deadline. The native people of the James Bay region were negotiating under the gun of a deadline to which they had to adhere. If they did not adhere, they and their people would suffer serious consequences.
They were negotiating also under the gun of a very difficult internal deadline. For example, one of the matters of the James Bay situation as those familiar with the facts know, had to do with the classification of various types of land and the limitations of use which would be applied against these various classifications. But the native people of that region were forced to settle the land classification questions early before the deadline, and they knew very well that if they did not meet
James Bay Agreement
that deadline, the decisions as to their land classification would be taken unilaterally by people who did not have, as they have demonstrated throughout this affair, the interest of the native peoples at heart. Nor did they understand the circumstances and history of the native peoples of that region.
Finally, they were forced to negotiate under the gun of extraordinary conditions, conditions to which people of a different kind of background would probably not have been subjected. One of those, for example, had to do with the fact that the government of Quebec made it clear from the outset that there would be no agreement by the government of Quebec without the consent of Quebec Hydro. Quebec Hydro indicated that it would agree only if the Inuit people who were affected would accept conditions which denied in advance their right to invoke social impact factors of proposed future hydroelectric projects. In other words, when the native people came to the table to negotiate, they were told that the negotiation would proceed only if they agreed to give up their right to raise objections to the social and environmental impacts of unspecified future hydroelectric developments. That was a great deal to ask! It was, in my judgment, an unreasonable imposition to place upon the native peoples of that place at that time. But that was another of the conditons into which they were forced to enter in those negotiations.
That combination of deadlines and special conditions, imposed upon an unsophisticated people forced to negotiate about their future and their children's future in the middle of a modern metropolis, was bad enough in itself. That would be bad enough to raise the concern of any Canadian interested in justice. What makes the matter worse and makes it a matter for the attention and concern of the House of Commons of Canada is that the people who are involved here are by law the trust responsibility of the government of Canada.
Throughout this event, from the day the Liberal prime minister of Quebec decided to proceed until there was an agreement acquiesced in by the Liberal government of Canada, there was an abdication of federal responsibility that is simply repugnant to anyone who honours the law or wants to establish a basis of trust on which we might build respect and strength for the native people in this country.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext:
As I have said before, a great number of the people in the James Bay region fall directly under the responsibility of the government of Canada. That is made explicit in section 2(c) of the 1912 Quebec Boundaries Extension Act, which states in subsection (e):
That the trusteeship of the Indians in the said territory, and the management of any lands now or hereafter reserved for their use, shall remain in the government of Canada subject to the control of parliament.
That is absolutely clear. There can be no doubt about the responsibility of the government of Canada for the people who were involved in the James Bay region. However, instead of exercising that responsibility to a people who were imperilled,

December 14, 1976
James Bay Agreement
the federal government abandoned its solemn legal trust and adopted, instead, a policy which they called alert neutrality. Alert neutrality is hardly an adequate way for this or any government to carry out fundamental responsibilities to people in a field where progress will be made only if there is active trust and active co-operation instead of alert neutrality.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Instead of sending moral support and federal expertise, expertise of the law officers of the federal crown which the natives in that region had a right to expect, the federal Liberal government sent money by the back door in dribs and drabs and in amounts of which the total was insufficient. In the debate in the House of Commons at that time, I called it conscience money because this government knew that they had not done their duty. They had abandoned the people to whom they had responsibility. They felt sufficiently guilty about if that they dribbled in some public payments in the form of conscience money. In retrospect, when we look upon the precedent that might have been set and the extent of abandonment of responsibility, that was far too generous a term.
We all recognize that in the circumstances the native people who were abandoned by their guardians did very well in the negotiations they were able to cause by their actions in the court, negotiations that they carried on in unfamiliar circumstances and under very difficult conditions. They won many concessions. I and my colleagues in this House of Commons want to pay tribute to the tremendous effort that was made by the members of the Grand Council of the Cree. They clearly worked against extensive odds. They did a very good job in achieving concessions under those kinds of circumstances and those unrealistic deadlines imposed by the Liberal government. However, the process itself simply does not merit the approval which is asked for in the title of this bill. 1 suggest it does not even merit the tolerance of the parliament of Canada.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext:
I will not take a great deal of time reviewing all the aspects of this legislation. However, I want to draw to the attention of the House some of the serious deficiencies that exist in the provisions of the agreement-deficiencies, as the minister suggested in his opening remarks-that might be corrected, or at least some of them. These deficiencies cause us as a parliament exercising our responsibility to take a very serious look at this bill.
In passing, I want to make it clear that whatever the content of the bill, it is our judgment that this parliament cannot let pass the process which gave rise to this bill without protest. As the hon. member for Lambton-Kent, in a very eloquent speech the other night, made clear and as I and others who take part in this debate today and later will make clear, we intend to protest to the extent of our ability the irresponsible way in which the government of Canada abandoned its responsibility to the native people of the James Bay region.
(Mr. Clark.]
Let us look at some of the deficiencies that now exist in the agreement. I will not try to enumerate all of them. However, they include the fact that two small tribes, the Naskapis and the Montagnais, are not included in the agreement. They are nomadic and follow the caribou herd between Quebec and Labrador. They are people whose traditional roots are in that region. They belong as much to the James Bay region as others who are there. The government maintains they are covered under the agreement, but the Indians concerned believe that they are not. While they are not recognized as treaty Indians specifically, it is clear that the federal government had been involved with them before. It had accepted a certain responsibility for them when their problems were minor. However, when their problems became major, when it became a question of their future and their very right to carry on in the traditional way they and their forefathers had known for generations, they were cut adrift by the government of Canada. They are left adrift by the agreement we are called upon to approve today.
In his opening remarks, the minister said he was prepared to again sit down with them to see if some sort of amendment could be worked out. However, at the very most that involves inclusion after the fact in an agreement that they had no opportunity to influence. Another of the deficiencies in the agreement before us is that it has become the cause of very serious reservations among certain of the Inuit communities which are involved in the land, in particular the residents of three communities, Sugluk, Ivugivik and Povungnituk. They are concerned about the effect of this legislation upon their future. The government might say, "What matter are they? There are only 1,200 people in these three communities, out of a total community of 4,000." However, I say to this parliament and the government of Canada that when this parliament and this government begins to count as inconsequential 1,200 native people, we have betrayed the responsibilities that we as legislators have in a free society.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext:
The people of these three communities are sufficiently unhappy with this agreement that they are now seeking to sever their relationship with the Northern Quebec Inuit Association.
In terms of deficiencies in the bill, the minister in his speech boasted, and 1 think it is fair to say it was a boast, that the native people in that region were given what he called an equal voice in certain development matters: they were given an equal voice in the industry in determining ways to remedy the impact of hydro activities south of the fifty-fifth parallel; they were given an equal voice with government in administering and supervising the social and environmental impact studies throughout the region. That is one way of phrasing it the way the minister did. The other way, the honest way, is to say that the companies and the governments have an equal voice with the natives. It requires no imagination to know whose will is going to prevail when questions arise regarding the social and environmental impact of proposals brought forward by the
December 14, 1976

companies and the governments which are granted by this legislation an equal voice with the native people whose lives are affected.
It is very clear that as hard and as effectively as the Grand Council of Cree worked throughout this, it is highly likely that the agreement we are dealing with today would be very different if the native people involved had had adequate resources and were not forced to meet deadlines of the sort imposed upon them under the threat of imposition of conditions. It is also quite clear, in my judgment, that if they had received the support of the federal government to which they were entitled, instead of this cop-out policy of alert neutrality, we would today have been dealing with an agreement very different from this one, an agreement which would have been much more in the interests of the native people involved.
Another area of concern is that the ratification vote was rushed through. The agreement was translated into the native tongue only at the last minute, and only under pressure. Then the translation document was circulated in conditions under which it was difficult to ensure adequate information or real consensus. The document was circulated in abbreviated form.
Another matter which must be of concern to us was drawn to public attention by Mr. John Ciaccia, a member of the national legislative assembly for Mount Royal who represented the government of Quebec in these negotiations, having previously served as assistant deputy minister for Indian affairs in the government of Canada. Mr. Ciaccia said, in an article quoted in the Montreal Gazette of November 6, 1975, that "in effect the agreement would have precedence over the federal Indian Act". That is a statement by a member of the provincial legislature, then the provincial spokesman for a government, which must cause concern to members of a parliament of Canada which under the British North America Act retains exclusive legislative jurisdiction over the native people under section 91 of that act.
As I say, there are a number of specific areas in this bill which require correction. But it is the whole process of the approach to this legislation which is unacceptable to anyone who takes seriously the responsibility which falls upon the parliament of Canada for the native people as spelled out in the BNA Act. Even more important, we are not lawyers here: this is not merely a court or a house of lawyers; this is a body which is supposed to be concerned about social justice and it is supposed to come to the protection of any people who are seriously threatened, whether or not there is a legal obligation.
Against this background, we cannot allow to pass quietly a process which has involved the abandonment of people whose rights it was our responsibility to protect, a process which has involved taking advantage of people unaccustomed to the ways of lawyers and of Crown corporations, people whose leaders were brought down and forced to bargain away their heritage under pressure in the centre of a metropolis.
What most concerns me and members of my party is not just the content of the agreement, although we have some
James Bay Agreement
reservations about that. We are concerned particularly about the events which led to this bill, not because they stand alone but because they are, unhappily, symptomatic of the way the white majority society has earned the mistrust of the native people. We in the white majority talk a great deal about the rights and needs of native people. We do that in the abstract. But when the crunch comes and when the contest is between the Cree people and Quebec Hydro, it is Quebec Hydro which wins. When Ottawa is asked to exercise its solemn responsibility in the name of the principles it espouses, Ottawa backs down and abandons the people for whom it is responsible.
I recognize, as do others in the House, and as do many of the Indian leaders themselves, that native people are not always right.

Now and again their demands have been excessive. At times, their positions were based on nostalgia. Of course, there are those who have had some experience with the Indians in Canada. A minority of them are becoming extremists, and they have imported confrontation tactics from the United States.

But we must also recognize that whatever the weaknesses, whatever the problems, some of which individual native people may have brought upon themselves, to whatever degree they have failed to resist the slide into dependency which has been created for them by white society, they are working hard and seriously now to improve their situation. It is clear to anyone who has dealt with native people in Canada that native leadership has in the last two decades been exceptional in its sense of responsibility and in its wisdom, in its capacity to articulate its concern and its case.
While this example of leadership has been forthcoming from the minority, the majority in society, as demonstrated recently in the events leading up to this bill, has continued to apply a double standard of morality to these issues, using one standard when they talk and another when they act. Some of the glamour has gone out of the issue of native rights in the past few years. It is not the fashionable issue it once was. But it remains, for any Canadian parliament, a fundamental issue, one which tests the capacity of our society for justice and honest compromise. The government opposite has, throughout the life of its mandate, earned the mistrust of the native people of Canada.

HEALTH AND WELFARE
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING LIMITATION OF NOISE IN FACTORIES
speechtext:
that Bill C-209, an act respecting noise in factories, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is spelled out in the explanatory notes. Bill C-209 would require that the government of Canada stipulate as a condition of acceptability of any contract that the firm considered comply with the regulation that none of its workers would be subjected to a noise level greater than 85 dBA for an eight-hour period. Let me explain, Mr. Speaker, that dBA is the abbreviation for decibels on the "A" weighted scale. This scale is commonly used in measuring noise levels both of industrial and domestic articles. Noise is, up to a point, a qualitative category. Electronic rock music is to some unbearable and consequently noise, while to others this music is extremely pleasant and is not considered noise. However, the sounds we are talking of today, industrial noise, do not fall into this contentious area.
My remarks this afternoon will not be of a technical or jargonistic nature. I have neither the expertise nor the inclination to become involved in a discussion concerning the finer points of the scientific arguments in this area. Far too often, in my opinion, these exchanges are used to obfuscate the true issue concerned; that instead of proceeding to decide on the issue of noise abatement we would contribute to the already existing din. Talk thus far has provided very little protection for the people working in noisy industries. I hope some action today will help soothe their aching ears.
The fundamental issue to be resolved here is one of rights. I am sure that my hon. colleagues agree that workers should not have to risk one of their God-given senses as the price they must pay for the jobs they hold. There can be no question that a person has the right to work in an environment that is not harmful. Deafness is not a fair exchange for a job, Mr. Speaker.
Many doctors and scientists disagree about the short and long-term effects of noise. Some contend that illnesses exist, such as ulcers, which come as a direct result of continual and unwanted noise. Some argue that loud sounds cause nervousness, hypertension, mental exhaustion and high blood pressure. Researcher Hans Selye has suggested that noise may also cause stress that can result in a lowered resistance to infection.
Social Health
These theories are advocated by some physicians, others do not accept them. However, there can be no dispute that hearing impairment is a result of living and working in an industrial society.
Medically speaking, it is recognized that auditory loss is a result of damage to the minute hair cells in the inner ear. These hair cells transmit sound pressure along nerves to the brain. If they become impaired the connection will be faulty and even incomplete. High noise levels play a large role in damaging these hair cells. If a person is exposed to a loud sound, these cells tire and a temporary hearing loss could follow. When the noise is removed, hearing usually returns. On the other hand, if the noise is consistent for a period of months or years, these hair cells are destroyed and hearing damage is permanent. A medical official of the Ontario Workman's Compensation Board reported that if workers were subjected to greater than 95 decibels for an eight-hour period, it could be predicted that the worker very well could be deaf in five years, if the sound was maintained at that level.
Reaction to noise falls into two categories. If a person is exposed to constant noise, his ear has the ability to adjust for a short period of time. In an article entitled "Noise is a Health Hazard" Dr. Roy Chatterton explains that while an ear can cut off some of the unwanted noise, after a half hour this reflex fatigues. There is no natural protection for impulse noise, however. Impulse noise is defined as sudden unexpected and irregular sound, such as gunfire. The ear cannot protect itself from this type. It cannot turn off; consequently far more damage is done. Impulse noises produce vibrations so intense that tissue inside the ear can be literally torn apart.
The obvious solution to these problems would be to prohibit sounds that induce this reaction deafness. Unfortunately, there is no universal benchmark for the beginning of hearing loss. Each person reacts to sound differently. Some people are more sensitive to noise than others. Some regulations do exist to provide a modicum of protection for workers in noisy industries.
The Canadian Labour Code noise regulations, which apply to federal government's businesses, allow a worker to be exposed to 87 to 90 decibels for an eight-hour day. For six hours he may be exposed to anything from 90 to 92 decibels. The provinces of Ontario, British Columbia and Quebec have similar regulations that allow for eight hours per day. The province of Alberta is, however, a forerunner in worker protection.
