You might say "Naturally", but at least it is the forerunner. Regulations under the workman's compensation act and the public health safety act in this province specify that a sound level of 85 decibels is permissible for an eight-hour day, and at 90 decibels the permitted exposure time is four hours. Prince Edward Island, Nova Scotia and Newfoundland do not have stipulated sound levels. Rather, they

December 14, 1976
Social Health
require protective equipment where noise levels are judged to be excessive, harmful or injurious. The absence of established statutory exposure levels leaves the efficacy of these regulations open to subjective interpretation.
In the United States, the Walsh-Healey regulation sets maximum levels of 90 decibels for an eight-hour shift. However, the environmental protection agency has been charged with the responsibility of carrying on research into environmental noise and has, as a result, advocated a reduction to 85 decibels. In support of this is the occupational safety and health administration. A survey completed by the occupational safety and health administration came up with telling and, I believe, convincing results. Taking into account extra work noise, the occupational safety and health administration discovered that of the 14 million workers studied, 1.7 million or 12 per cent would suffer from hearing impairment after 40 years of work. If the decibel was strictly limited to 90, this number would be reduced to 1 million or 7 per cent. If, however, an 85-decibel limit was maintained, only 200,000 of those 14 million, or 1.5 per cent, would incur hearing damage. Certainly this is not perfect, but a 1.5 per cent margin is a reasonable target that should not only be aimed for but achieved.
Some hon. members may well wonder whether a five-decibel decrease will change anything. I say it will, for this reason. The method used to compute sound pressure levels is calculated logarithmically. When the intensity of a sound is doubled, it appears only as a three-decibel increase, that is, from 85 to 88 decibels. Five decibels, therefore, represents a considerable decrease in the noise level, a decrease that will benefit workers immensely.
As the occupational safety and health administration study indicated, a reduction of the acceptable noise level would drastically decrease the number of potential cases of hearing impairment. When the province of Ontario has paid out an average of $910,000 per year for the past five years to workers suffering from some sort of hearing impairment, something must be done. When in Ontario, in 1975, there were 639 pensions granted because of hearing loss, this situation must be remedied.
As I stated earlier, it is the intention of Bill C-209 to set guidelines for potential federal tenders. Noise regulations do fall under provincial jurisdiction. This does not mean, though, that the federal government can ignore its responsibility. There are precedents for provinces accepting the form of federal legislation and incorporating it into their own statutes. A current example is consumer protection legislation. Consequently, the federal government's adoption of this measure may well encourage provinces to follow suit, and in the meantime could protect industrial workers who it would otherwise be powerless to help.
So far I have discussed the causes of short and long-term deafness, noise-related illnesses, provincial and U.S. regulations, and the effects the reduction would have. It is necessary to examine the consequences an 85-decibel limit would have on the industries concerned. Objections have been raised that this

noise level would impose serious hardships on industry; that 85 decibels is technologically or economically not feasible. Industry spokesmen contend that, particularly for older plants, this program would be prohibitively expensive. Their complaint bears some consideration.
I would recommend, if hon. members see fit to send this bill to the committee, that when a regional safety officer states it is not reasonably practical for an employer to comply with the 85-decibel limit, the employer would be required to provide hearing protectors for his staff. The protectors would have to be of the variety that reduce the sound reaching the employees' ears to less than 85 decibels.
Several factors must be considered with regard to the cost to industry. However, Dr. Nicholas Ashford, from the Centre for Policy-Alternatives at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, has made a study comparing health costs and industry's cost to comply with the 90 and 85-decibel limits. Dr. Ashford discovered when a dollar value was placed on workmen's compensation, absenteeism, and mental annoyance, after 40 years an 85-decibel limit would in fact be cheaper than a 90-decibel limit. Dr. Ashford, who prepared his brief for the Ford Foundation, said:
-many companies could save more (by reducing noise) than the workmen's compensation premiums associated with claims relating to occupational deafness. Noise also reduces the level of visual acuity, with the result that the cost of accidents and shoddy workmanship, is likely to be higher in noisy shops.
The American department of labour, in a report completed by acoustic experts, concluded that an 85 decibel limit could be achieved for at least 92 per cent of production workers. If hon. members so decide, I would recommend to the committee that 85 decibels be the maximum allowable level in industries having federal contracts. I would also suggest that if workers had to perform in noisier conditions, time of exposure should be reduced in accordance with the intensity of sound.
It is also necessary to ensure that industries do not have to bear excessive responsibilities. Consequently, when it is beyond the ability of employers to reasonably reduce sound pressure levels, I would suggest that the employer provide the staff with CSA approved hearing protectors and that warning signs be posted explaining noise levels. It is also advisable that anyone employed in an excessive noise area undergo regularly audiometric testing so that early signs of deterioration can be detected.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, let me say that legislation of this kind is long overdue. Too many people fearing loss of their jobs have tolerated noise levels which have permanently damaged their hearing, rather than seek aid and compensation. At a time when the technology exists to prevent such tragedies, we should make as great an effort as possible to provide protection for people who work to provide so many of society's necessities.
At 85 decibels a conversation can be carried on at three feet, shouting, so what is being suggested is not the quiet of a library. High noise levels have proved dangerous to hearing;
December 14, 1976

they also impair efficency and industrial safety. I urge my hon. colleagues to support this measure which will put a little humanity into the workplace. With regard to deafness, Helen Keller said:
Ours is not the silence that soothes the weary sense. It is an inhuman silence which severs and estranges. It is a silence which isolates cruelly and completely.
Let us protect as many as possible from this unnecessary burden. The Chair indicated that the bill should be referred to the Standing Committee on Health, Welfare and Social Affairs, but I ask that it be referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.

Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to speak briefly on Bill C-209. I want to commend the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) for proposing this legislation. I must confess to him that when I first saw that there was a bill dealing with noise pollution, I thought it was to reform the rules of the House. I was pleasantly surprised to learn that the bill deals with the problem of noise pollution in factories.
The hon. member deserves a great deal of credit for the comments in his speech on second reading of the bill. 1 think he explained the bill extremely well. He made a good case for its passage, or at least for allowing it to be read a second time and to go to the committee where members can hear representations from labour and business as to the effects of the bill, and particularly the representations of business. As the hon. member explained, the purpose of the bill is to deal with the problem of noise pollution in industrial plants. He explained the bill quite fully, and I do not propose to take a great deal of time. I certainly do not want to be responsible for preventing the bill from coming to a vote this afternoon.
There is a growing recognition on the part of Canadians throughout this country that there are tremendous problems caused by noise pollution in factories and by noise pollution generally. In recent years there has been an awareness of the problems of environmental health hazards and of the effects that noise pollution can have on one's hearing, on one's general health and also upon one's ability to work. The fact is that studies have shown that where workers are asked to work under conditions which are unfavourable and which are very unpleasant for them, the quality of their work deteriorates. Anything we as a parliament can do to improve employment standards for people in Canada and to improve their productivity and health should be done.
I think there is also a general recognition on the part of business that anything that can be done by businesses to improve the working conditions of their employees should be done, and I think there is a willingness to comply wherever possible with what is being suggested in this bill. 1 think the hon. member recognized in the comments he made that there would be instances in which there would be difficulties for industries in complying with the provisions of the bill. Obviously, there are some industries in which it is simply impossible-for example, in heavy industries dealing with metal or in industries where people work around aircraft-to lower the noise level to below 85 decibels. However, the hon. member
Social Health
quite properly suggested that in those instances the employees involved should be provided with protective devices which would give some protection to their eardrums and which would prevent them from being damaged. If the provisions of the bill were applied flexibly, no undue burden need be put upon employers. The bill could also do a great deal to encourage employers who really are not concerned about the well-being of their employees to take some action.
The hon. member noted that under the terms of the British North America Act it is likely that the responsibility for legislation with regard to noise levels in industry falls under provincial jurisdiction. Obviously, the parliament of Canada cannot legislate a national standard for noise pollution in factories and force it upon the provinces. To do so would be improper and an intrusion on provincial jurisdiction. It would obviously be illegal, as well. However, what the hon. member tries to do in his bill is come in, perhaps through the back door, and set standards of behaviour for factories which are doing work on behalf of the federal government. That might encourage the provinces to take some action as well. I think that is a sensible way of dealing with this problem.
This bill would only take effect in cases where there are federal contracts involved with industries, and this could be a condition of the contracts. I do not think, in my reading of the bill, that this maximum noise level is compulsory in all contracts, but it could be a condition of a contract between the federal government and a private employer that the noise level in the factory to which employees would be subjected would have to be 85 decibels or lower. I think the hon. member is acting in a responsible way.
At the outset I promised that my remarks would be very brief. Let me just say again that the hon. member deserves credit for having introduced the bill. I think it would be worth while to have a much closer study of it. At the committee stage it would be possible to call expert witnesses who could testify as to the health hazards involved and as to whether the level of 85 decibels is a sensible level, and it would also be possible for us to have representatives of business and labour explain their perspectives on the problem.
I recommend that the House give favourable consideration to this bill, and I want to say, again, to the hon. member that I feel he has made a good start on the bill. I hope the House will look favourably on allowing the bill to go to committee.

I think it is a fact of history in this country that the federal labour code and the provincial labour codes tend to run along in parallel courses. There is a fair amount of co-operation between the federal Department of Labour and the various provincial departments of labour, and I think that if pressure could be exerted for all of these codes to establish more effective regulations regarding noise, we would be doing the right thing.

We have to act on all fronts.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I may, I would like first of all to congratulate the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) for having introduced Bill C-209 which will allow us to explain what this bill is all about and what the government is doing to reduce noise in factories.
The purpose of this bill is to find a way to reduce industrial noise in establishments having contracts with the government of Canada or provincial governments. In most of these establishments, the type of work, undertaking or business do not fall under the legislative authority of Parliament, that is under federal government jurisdiction to which federal laws apply generally.
Except in broiler manufactures and other establishments of this type which are always extraordinarily noisy, the adverse effects on human hearing has not been understood until recent years, and therefore no one was greatly concerned about controlling this occupational risk before 1956. Considering the circumstances outlined in the above paragraph, it is not surprising that only two provinces, British Columbia and Alberta, prescribed and energically enforce noise control regulations as detailed as the Canada Noise Control Regulations which have been in force since November 2, 1971 and which apply to all work sites subject to federal authority and governed by Part IV of the Labour Code of Canada, entitled Safety of Employees.
In most provinces, general noise regulations have been implemented, the main principle of which is as follows:
All employers must ensure that all measures which are practically achievable, in the opinion of an inspector, are taken to prevent any impairment of hearing in an industry, by reducing or eliminating the noise produced by any machine or device.
An important step toward the universal adoption of detailed noise control regulations was made with the issuing of a standard noise code by the federal-provincial committee of deputy ministers of labour. This standard code is used as a guide by various authorities to draft noise control regulations. Companies or entreprises which are not subject to federal authority and which carry out projects under federal contracts must conform to the local or provincial conditions that apply in their case. The contractors concerned have to comply with provincial regulations and, under the contract, they may also have to comply with any additional requirement the federal government might impose if provincial regulations were considered inadequate.
Bill C-209 is inadequate because it provides only for one noise ceiling. The evaluation of the dangers of hearing impairment due to noise is a very intricate process and it must take into consideration not only the intensity of the noise but also its frequency, its acuity and the length of the period of
December 14, 1976

exposure to this noise. For example, in many plants, the intensity of the noise could exceed 85 decibels without being dangerous to the employees because of its intermittence. The sound levels, the details of exposure and the other requirements of Canada anti-noise regulations are the outcome of ample research and consulting and they are based on international standards which proved efficient in ensuring some protection against hearing troubles attributable to noise in the working environment.
In addition to the inspector service to ensure compliance with Canada anti-noise regulations, federal or provincial security agents and other experts are available to analyze the problems caused by noise and to advise as to remedial actions to be taken where necessary. Bill C-209 tends to solve the problem of jurisdiction posed by its predecessor, Bill C-247, by requiring that the provisions relating to noise level be part of any government contract for the performance of work. So, this bill is in fact directed to the government and its purpose could be met through administrative channels.
As the present bill would have the effect of requiring that the evaluation of health and security conditions on the working sites of the contractor be considered as a factor in awarding government contracts, it would then be in line with the government objectives for health and security matters in working places under its responsibility.
To achieve this, however, the bill should provide for the inspection of working areas of other contractors, so that comparative assessment of respective conditions could be made. This would necessitate the establishment of criteria more detailed than the mere 85 decibel level indicated in Bill C-209 to evaluate hearing damage hazards. Appropriate criteria could be found in the Canadian regulations governing the fight against excessive noise.
Since the introduction of Bill C-209 has been clearly prompted by a concern for the health of plant workers, we can certainly wonder why it has been set on such a narrow basis which causes it to deal only with noise. It should conceivably deal also with the many health hazards which are likely to be found in the working areas of government contractors. Any effort to force these contractors to comply with Part IV of the Canadian Labour Code and the relevant regulations would face strong opposition from the provinces, which would accuse the federal government of meddling with matters under provincial jurisdiction.
While I appreciate the hon. member's concern, I feel this bill is not acceptable, because its aims could better be achieved by extending the area of application of the current legislation and by seeking the adoption of universal health and safety standards by all authorities concerned.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to give a number of examples which we come across in our every day life. There are days when there is so much noise in the House that, if we were to apply the 85 decibel level criterion, the House would be compelled to adjourn. Yet, no one could claim that the current noise level should prevent us from sitting. I should like also to suggest to the hon. member that noise level inside an industry
Social Health
or a plant can reflect on productivity, and that it will not necessarily limit the capacity of an employee or help him earn a living.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that in spite of some flows we have every power from an administrative point of view to implement proposals expressed in Bill C-209 and it is not necessary to pass another legislation to spell out the rights of plant employees when it comes to noise level.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING LIMITATION OF NOISE IN FACTORIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my colleague from Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) for what I think is a most timely legislation in a period when we must question all our labour union system in Canada.
I also want to congratulate the member for Longueuil (Mr. Olivier) for his outstanding speech, which was both technical and very sound, and I believe that his last words prove the deep concern of a man who was himself a former trade unionist. When he mentioned the word "productivity" in relating it with the quality of life which must be granted to workers inside a plant, we see in this man someone who knows the interests of Canadian workers and continues to defend them.
Mr. Speaker, in answering the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, I pointed out at some length this question of productivity and of quality of life for the workers. I mentioned that we should question all our process of collective negotiations, and to realize this we should have both employers and unions sit and reestablish priorities which are usually negotiated. Unfortunately, these last years in Canada we have been negotiating collective agreements in which labour demands were mainly aimed at salary increases, without considerations being given to the well being of workers.
Bill C-209 concerns noise. We can also talk, as in the case of Thetford Mines, about the hazards threatening those who work in asbestos mines. In fact, according to some statistics, it is interesting to note that Canada now enforces ever more severe security standards and yet never has the rates of accidents been so high. It is thus difficult to understand that although our security standards are more consistent and better than in the past, the accident rates are spiraling upwards, which obviously has a direct effect on productivity which decreases day after day.
So I believe that the crucial problem we will face within a few years will concern productivity. It is thus necessary that governments, employers and unions meet around a table to redefine better means to improve productivity, taking into account the quality of the worker's life and respecting the human being and not only worrying about the use of capital. In fact, I think that money, though important, does not give the estimated results if not used while respecting the individual.
Now I think that bills such as this one should be incorporated into a series of measures that would go far beyond that, which would try to give the average worker a sense of dignity, so that he may give his best and contribute more to the Canadian economy.

December 14, 1976
Social Health
We will have to face a labour shortage from the 80s onward. Our problem in Canada will no longer unemployment. The Economic Council of Canada agrees with that: there will be a shortage of workers. Then it is quite obvious that if we have to face that shortage and at the same time open our doors wider to immigration, we will have then to deal with people who are not used to the working facilities available in Canada. It is obvious that, in view of the scarcity of manpower, unions will no longer have to struggle so much about getting higher wages. I trust they will then be willing to negotiate working conditions that will give back some dignity to the worker and, in fact, motivate him to produce more and better.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in view of these data, I feel the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore should ask the House instead to have the committee on labour, manpower and immigration hear experts, whether they be from the International Labour Office in Geneva, or union representatives to arrive at basic criteria through which we can give back the plant worker some measure of self-respect.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, to my mind such a meeting is necessary and would be that much more timely that the wage and price control program is about to end. Obviously, ome unions are now in the process of negotiating collective agreements, and some companies are doing so, aware that when controls are lifted the workers will get increases that would conflict with present standards. Naturally, if we practice that kind of labour relations, and if the employer signs that kind of agreement, he is working against his own interests.
And to settle a particular dispute, they are going to jeopardize all the success our program has achieved since it was brought into operation. But, Mr. Speaker, it is essential that an employer-employee organization should no longer be concerned only with the individual interest of each of these groups, but also with the future of our Canadian economy. And it is not through practices as those we have known in the past that we are going to build a strong economy supported by a strong industrial framework. It would be more advisable to readjust our aims, bring work into favour again and define new priorities.
Mr. Speaker, again I want to congratulate my colleague the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore but, as I said earlier, I do not think that we should deal only with the problem of noise pollution, but also with the general working conditions, with all possible means to make the worker happier so that, by himself, he will accept to produce more and better serve his country.

subtopic: HEALTH AND WELFARE
subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING LIMITATION OF NOISE IN FACTORIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too would like to join my colleagues and commend the hon. member for Toronto-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson) for his concern about our quality of life. This is the third time he has introduced legislation about attaining a better quality of life. I remember that one of his first bills was designed to create a non-smoker section on aircraft and public transportation systems. We are grateful to our colleague for realizing the importance of the

application of such a concept to airlines and other public transportation.
Going over the bill I see that hon. member has limited his intention to decibels, but I am sure he would want to go beyond this. That is precisely what I should like the hon. member to do, and I hope to assist him in making sure that the provisions of this bill go beyond the decibel limit to which people can be exposed for a certain period of time.
What I mean by this, Mr. Speaker, is that the definition of a work site or a contract for the federal government is a somewhat complex matter since jobs for the federal government are not done exclusively within plants.
I would give as an example the work now being done on Wellington Street, about 160 feet from my office in the Confederation Building. I am on the second floor and the horrendous noise made by the drills is simply unbearable. We had to ask the maintenance man and the Department of Public Works to install sound-proof panels against our windows to enable the young office girls to work without getting terrible headaches every day, since this noise is heard every day from eight in the morning until six in the evening. This is one of the problems about which my colleague for Toronto-Lakeshore certainly did not think sufficiently, Mr. Speaker, that is the definition of a framework of jobs to be done for the federal government.
It might also be a good idea to extend the legislation sufficiently to include other areas, not necessarily where work is done for the federal government, but where the public is exposed to unsettling noises or noises which are louder that the acceptable decibel level. I am thinking, for instance, Mr. Speaker, of what we must suffer when we enter discotheques. It is not necessarily those who go to discotheques who suffer most because they do so voluntarily to amuse themselves. But I am thinking about the employees, about the young girls and boys who wait on tables and who must endure that infernal amplified music which so very often exceeds the number of decibels we have mentioned, that is 85, 115 or 120.
There are also other places where people are exposed to noises whose frequency can do much greater damage than impulse noises and, for example, would exceed a certain number of decibels, as in the case of jet airplanes flying directly above when taking off or landing. That is one of the reasons why, when the federal government decided to set up a second airport in the Montreal area, we wanted to expropriate no fewer than 78,000 acres so that people living around the airport or under its air corridors would not be unduly affected by the noise, but if they were they could always move elsewhere without financial losses.
Mr. Speaker, this is an aspect of the problem that I do not think my colleague for Toronto-Lakeshore has considered seriously.
December 14, 1976

There is also the question of jurisdiction over working conditions in Canada. According to my sources, Mr. Speaker, conditions pertaining to work, health and security on job sites or in factories come under the exclusive jurisdiction of provincial governments. I do not think that many would accept to give up readily this jurisdiction in favour of the federal government so that it may enforce this piece of legislation limiting the number of decibels to which workers can be exposed.
Within federal jurisdiction, the Canadian Labour Code has limited the number of decibels in a work area. If we read the Canadian Labour Code of November 1971, as amended on January 1973, we see that it limits the number of decibels for the number of hours of work that may be expected of an employee.
There is no doubt, Mr. Speaker, that the provisions of the Canada Labour Code are not enough because there are places where the federal government does not have jurisdiction to enforce those constraints. On the other hand, as my hon. colleague for Chambly (Mr. Loiselle) indicated earlier, and as the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour pointed out, that area falls under exclusive provincial jurisdiction and it is hard to see how the federal government could impose its view in this area through legislation. Furthermore, the lack of enthusiasm on the part of the provinces to impose federal views in such areas should not be forgotten.
So I believe, Mr. Speaker, that it might be preferable for each province to pass legislation to deal with that problem and thus limit the hazards to which workers are exposed as a result of noises exceeding acceptable decibel limits.

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Allmand that Bill C-9, to approve, give effect to and declare valid certain agreements between the Grand Council of Crees (of Quebec), the Northern Quebec Inuit Association, the Government of Quebec, la Societe d'energie de la Baie James, la Societe de developpement de la Baie James, la Commission hydro-electrique de Quebec and the Government of Canada and certain other related agreements to which the Government of Canada is a party, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Indian Affairs and Northern Development.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to speak on what I believe to be a very historic bill, historic because it is a bill to confirm a major settlement of a land claim by some 10,000 native people in the province of Quebec. I believe it is the first time since confederation that such a bill has been brought before parliament and parliament called upon to consider such a settlement.
The minister has urged a quick passage of the bill. It is not the intention of our party to prolong the debate, but I would suggest that the bill deserves very serious consideration by members on all sides of the House.
In speaking in the debate on Tuesday, December 7 last, the minister traced the history of the native claims or native rights in the province of Quebec. He spoke of a bill that was passed
2010

December 14, 1976
James Bay Agreement
in 1891, 61 Victoria, chapter three, which was a very straightforward bill. It extended the boundary of the province of Quebec at that time to the Eastmain River.
The minister also spoke of a bill of 1912, the Boundaries Extension Act of 1912. That bill extended the boundaries north from the Eastmain River to the Northwest Territories. It is interesting to note that unlike the bill of 1898, that bill recognized the rights of the native peoples of the province of Quehec, specifically in the area that was ceded to the province at that time.
I would like to read into the record the excerpt from the act that spells out and recognizes the rights of the native people. It is referred to in Section 2, subsections (c), (d) and (e). Subsection (e) reads as follows:
That the province of Quebec will recognize the rights of the Indian inhabitants in the territory above described to the same extent, and will obtain surrenders of such rights in the same manner, as the Government of Canada has heretofore recognized such rights and has obtained surrender thereof, and the said province shall bear and satisfy all charges and expenditure in connection with or arising out of such surrenders:
Subsection (e) reads:
That the trusteeship of the Indians in the said territory, and the management of any lands now or hereafter reserved for their use, shall remain in the Government of Canada subject to the control of parliament.
That was in 1912. What took place in the meantime in negotiating the claims of the native people? Nothing transpired until almost 60 years later. It was not until 1971 when Premier Bourassa, the then premier of the province of Quebec, on his birthday, April 29, announced a multi-million dollar project, the largest single industrial project ever to be conceived in Canada and possibly in North America, that any thought was given to the claims of the native people. The premier made his announcement without any thought as to the effect such a project would have on the environment. He made it without considering the obligations of the province of Quebec to the native people under the act of 1912. It was only with the announcement by Premier Bourassa that the federal government became interested. As reported at page 1753 of Hansard the minister had this to say:
In October, 1971, the federal government provided funds to the Indians of Quebec Association to enable it to inform native people in the area about the proposed development. During the next two years the main effort was directed toward persuading the provincial government to address itself more directly to the concerns expressed by the native population. In the meantime, my predecessors gave both moral and financial support to the Indians.
I should like to draw attention particularly to the words "moral and financial support". I ask you, Mr. Speaker, whether the government, in giving "moral and financial support" was carrying out its responsibility as laid down in the act of 1912, namely, to exercise trusteeship over the native people in the area ceded to the province?
It is interesting to note that clause 7 of the bill we are discussing tonight repeals that portion of the 1912 legislation which provides for the exercise of trusteeship on the part of the federal government on behalf of the native people. In other words, when this bill is passed the government will have

abandoned its trusteeship as far as these native people are concerned.
What was the situation in 1971 after the province of Quebec had announced the project? On one side there were 10,000 native people, 6,000 of whom were Cree and 4,000 Inuit. On the other side there was ranged the might of the provincial government and of the Crown corporations-the James Bay Development Corporation, the James Bay Energy Corporation and the Quebec Hydro Corporation. And what action did the federal government take? It gave its "moral and financial support". Notwithstanding its trusteeship obligations it took no active part. I suggest this amounted to a complete abdication of responsibility under the provisions of the act of 1912.
We all know what happened next. The Cree applied to Mr. Justice Malhouf for an interim injunction to stop the work which was taking place in the northern part of Quebec. An interim injunction was granted. The province and the various corporations appealed the decision and the Court of Appeal over-ruled Mr. Justice Malhouf. The native people were then faced with no alternative but to proceed with negotiations, and a deadline was set-November of 1976. They were told they must sign an agreement by that date or there would be no agreement and they would have to take whatever the province and the various corporations would give them. I am aware that the Cree met this deadline.
The Inuit people, whose settlements are scattered throughout the northern province, were in difficulty. In early November of 1976 it was brought to my attention that the Inuit people wanted an extension of time in order to examine the proposed agreement further and discuss it among themselves. I approached the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and asked him whether he would arrange an extension of the deadline for at least a month. On November 6, 1975, I put the following question to the minister, as reported at page 8908 of Hansard:
In view of the fact that the draft agreement of settlement with the native people in the James Bay area is being considered by a standing committee of the Quebec Assembly, in view of the fact that hearings will continue until at least the end of this week in order to deal with the matter and since meaningful negotiations cannot take place during that period of time, will the minister not consider extending the time so as to enable the Inuit people to complete their negotiations?
To which the then minister, now the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Buchanan), replied:
It is my understanding that negotiations will be conducted again tomorrow and over the weekend with the Inuit people. That was my information as late as yesterday. I think we may really find a way to accommodate the concern that they secure some additional time.
There was no additional time granted. The deadline was November 11 and that is when the native people were forced to sign the agreement. I suggest that the agreement was signed under compulsion because the feeling was that if it were not signed there was a possibility the natives would be obliged to take whatever crumbs were thrown to them by the other interested parties.
Speaking in the debate on December 7, the minister sought to indicate that the agreement had met with the approval of
December 14, 1976

the Cree and the Inuit people. He mentioned percentages of native people who had voted and percentages of those who had approved the agreement. I shall not take the time of the House to repeat those figures. They speak for themselves.
The bill is going to committee shortly and I expect there will be a thorough and comprehensive study made of it at that time. Witnesses will be called, and 1 am sure it will be interesting to listen to the evidence they give. The agreement is a lengthy one. I trust that the minister and his officials will give us detailed explanations, setting forth the responsibilities and obligations of each of the two levels of government involved. I assume they will also explain how these obligations are to be carried out.
There is another question that comes to my mind, and that is what happens to this agreement and to the native people covered by it if the province of Quebec should separate? What will the obligations be at that point in time? It might be said that this question is hypothetical. It might be suggested that separation will take place and that I have encouraged it. I am not doing that, and I will do my utmost to see that separation is avoided, but we as politicians cannot put our heads in the sand. As responsible politicians we must consider these possibilities. We must face the fact that Premier Levesque is committed to separation. We must face the fact also that the federal government is the trustee for the native people in northern Quebec covered by this James Bay agreement.
I would hope that the minister and the government do not look upon this agreement as being a precedent for any settlement that might take place in the Northwest Territories or the Yukon territory. It is my belief that the government thinks it will be. We must recognize that the situation in the Territories and the Yukon is different than it was in northern Quebec. In the Territories there is a great public awareness of the situation. For the last year and a half or two years there have been the Berger commission hearings, and the National Energy Board hearings taking place here in Ottawa. There has been an opportunity for individuals, public interest groups, and others to have their input. There has been time for a breather. It is completely unlike the situation in James Bay where an agreement was forced upon the native people by virtue of the time restrictions placed on them.
I believe, as do other residents in the north, and as I believe people in all good conscience throughout all of Canada believe, that any settlement which takes place with native people in any part of Canada must be a settlement that takes into consideration the culture and the way of life of those native people. It must take into consideration the fact that the old theory of paternalism has failed. It must take into consideration the fact that the native people must regain their selfrespect. This must be built up and encouraged, and any settlement must be based on the premise that it will provide an economic base for the native people in order that they may move away from the welfare system and dependence on the federal government.
James Bay Agreement
Returning to the bill, Mr. Speaker, I am concerned particularly with clause 4 which reads as follows:
Subject to sections 5 and 6, the Governor in Council may, by order, approve, give effect to and declare valid
(a) any supplementary agreement to which the Government of Canada is a
party that is intended to alter, revoke, replace or add to the Agreement;-
Then it goes on to refer to an agreement which may be made with the Naskapi Indians of Schefferville, Quebec, or any other group of Indians or Inuit people.
There is nothing wrong with having provisions in the bill to make changes from time to time if the circumstances so require, but what concerns me is that if you read clause 5 you will see it provides for the means by which parliament may deal with these changes. It provides for closure in that it provides for a debate of only five hours. It provides that any agreement entered into may become law with the approval of only one House. In other words, if the Commons refuses to approve an amendment to the agreement and the Senate passes it, it would become law. That is quite a change from the democratic system of government to which we are accustomed.
Any changes that may be made this agreement, or any alteration or renegotiation with the Naskapi Indians, for example, should be brought before this House and discussed like any other bill. Any means of dealing with such changes which are of vital importance, not only to the native people but to the rest of the population as well, I submit must be submitted to this House and dealt with in the normal manner, just as any other legislation is dealt with by the House and the Senate.
I see that my time is running short. There are other matters pertaining to the bill and the agreement that I could raise, but there are other members who wish to participate, so I will say in conclusion that I am looking forward to having the opportunity of taking part in committee hearings when the bill is referred there for consideration.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I cannot conscientiously vote for this bill and approve it. We must think of its inception. In 1971, Mr. Bourassa, the former premier of Quebec, desperately needed some issue to boost his not too high prestige. He needed something with drama, so with almost historic euphoria he produced this particular plan. It was to be the largest single industrial project ever launched in Canada. Certainly it was a huge project which was to be the key to the social reconstruction of a good deal of Quebec.
At the beginning it was supposed to cost $2 billion. The present estimate is that it will cost $16 billion, and this is something not unknown when this sort of project is considered. Although there was a lot of publicity about it, the normal precautions were not taken. There were no adequate surveys, there were no consultations with the Indians, and there was no adequate debate in the legislature of Quebec nor, indeed, in this House. However, it was supposed to produce a great many jobs and so the deal has proceeded. Before it was approved, two task forces reported and advised either for delay or for abandonment of the project.
8000S-59y2

December 14, 1976
James Bay Agreement
I would like to ask the minister a few questions. He is not here, but I suppose he has good reasons not to be here when this important matter which is under his jurisdiction is under discussion.
One thing I would like to know is whether this government has consulted the new government of the province of Quebec. My recollection-and I cannot vouch for this-is that in the provincial legislature the Party Quebecois, then quite a small party, voted against approval of this particular agreement. Certainly Mr. Jacques Parizeau made many vigorous and pointed criticisms. Has the new government been consulted to see whether at this stage it is its desire to proceed? Is the new government in a position to commit $16 billion in capital to this project? What will this do to other projects the new government has? I think we have the right to know that.
I understand that the major purpose of this agreement was to provide electrical power for sale, largely in the United States of America. Are those sales going through as anticipated, or is the story we hear true, that the price being secured and the demands made are far less than expected? It may be too late to cancel the whole project, but is it too late to cut it down? I think we have the right to know, in view of the vast expansion of the expenditures, the sum to which this parliament will be committed if we pass this bill.
There is another factor about which I would like to know something. It is said that the power from this development is going to be used for the production of enriched uranium for sale to France. I understand it has been the policy of the federal government not to approve of the sale of enriched uranium to France. How does that stand? How will that affect the agreement which has been made? I think we have the right to ask that that be looked into.
I want to speak about the way this legislation has been introduced. The bill itself is very short and simple. It declares the agreement to be valid. It approves and gives effect to the agreement. Then comes this clause, which I think is significant in its tone as well as in its content:
All native claims, rights, title and interests, whatever they may be, in and to the Territory, of all Indians and all Inuit, wherever they may be, and all the native claims, rights, title and interests, whatever they may be, in Canada, of all the Inuit of Port Burwell are hereby extinguished . ..
Then it goes on to a clause which is not relevant at the present time. The main purpose of this legislation is to extinguish the rights of Indians. And what do they get in place of the rights which would be extinguished by the bill we are asked to approve? What they get is impossible to summarize. It is contained in an agreement of 452 pages, and a large number of them are totally unintelligible. I say that because I have tried to read the agreement.
This is the agreement the Inuit and the Cree are supposed to have approved. I do not know how they could approve it. Certainly I do not know how their approval could mean anything unless they understood what is in it, yet I defy any ordinary person, without calling lawyers, accountants, engineers and others, to go through the agreement in detail and to
[Mr. Brewing
say what it means. I resent, and I think this House ought to resent, the fact that we are being asked to approve of one simple little bill saying we approve of an agreement extinguishing the rights of these people in exchange for an agreement of 452 pages which is not subject to the approval, as I understand it, of this House, except in a general blanket way. It is not subject to amendment, although I understand that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) has said he would be ready to consider changes to the agreement. Of course he would have to negotiate them with the other parties to the agreement, including the province of Quebec.
We are faced with a fait accompli. We have no opportunity to get a reasonable understanding of this agreement. I know it is going to committee, but when this House is asked to deal with what has been described as one of the largest projects ever launched in this country, a project costing up to $16 billion, a large portion of which is committed by the Parliament of Canada, I think we have the right to know at least an outline of what is in this agreement. There may be a few hon. members in this House who have tried to read this agreement and who are in a position to explain it, but I doubt very much whether there are more than one or two at the very outside. Certainly the minister did not bother to try to explain it to the House.
Another thing which has to be borne in mind is whose land and whose lives we are dealing with. I understand we are dealing with only 10,000 people. Have we any right to deprive them of their livelihood? Have we any right to deprive them of their style of life just because there are relatively few of them? I acknowledge it is true that at certain stages in this agreement there are provisions for the benefit of the Indians. They are given a certain amount of local government, they are given rights of harvesting, and limited rights of fishing, hunting and trapping, but these are subject to all sorts of exceptions. I do not know whether these new rights which are handed to them are the same as, worse than, or better than the rights they have enjoyed since time immemorial. All I know is that the only place we can find them is in this long winded agreement.
This agreement is so complicated that it had to divide the relatively small amount of land involved into different categories. One category is simply for the exclusive use of the Indians, but it is interesting to note how big that category is. It is described by Mr. Ciaccia, who presented this agreement. I think he is a member of the legislature of Quebec. Certainly he was acting on its behalf. I am told he is the member of the national assembly for Mount Royal, and he was a special representative of Premier Robert Bourassa. He wrote a preface to the agreement in which he stated:
... the Category 1 lands ... represent a tiny portion of the whole territory. Approximately 3,250 square miles are to be allocated to the use of the Inuit, and 2,158 square miles to the use of the Crees. Thus, although these lands are vital to the native peoples and they constitute an essential element of the Quebec government's policy of protecting their traditional economy and culture, you will agree that they are of minimal importance in relation to the total economy 6f Quebec.
December 14, 1976

That is the kind of judgment we should be criticizing. The rights these people have depended upon for years are considered of minimal importance, and they are given a tiny proportion to use as their own in this category 1. Then there are categories 2 and 3. There are elaborate procedures with regard to the sale of bonds and with regard to the nature of compensation, and if I had time and thought the House would be interested, I would read some of the paragraphs about compensation, about the issuing of bonds and things of that kind. I defy anybody but expert corporation lawyers to have the vaguest idea of what the effect will be of words like "mortgage," "hypothec," and the like. If we cannot understand them, how can we expect the Cree and the Inuit to understand what is being done to them?
I think the minister, who is not here, is a conscientious and decent man, and he has said to this House that the Cree have approved of this and that at least some of the Inuit have signed the document. I am not so clear as to whether they have really approved or whether they do now approve. Other speakers have dwelt on the circumstances in which they had their backs against the wall when they gave their approval, and I have tried to stress the fact that approval of something you do not understand is hardly approval at all.
This is only one more chapter in the long, tragic history of the way the rights of the native peoples have been abused in this country. It is shameful episode after shameful episode. I know that some of the agreements are reasonably satisfactory, and some of the Indian groups in north Saskatchewan approve of the treaties they have. The only thing they do not approve of is that the government does not live up to the agreements, which of course is another way of making these agreements absolutely meaningless.
I want to say a word about trustees. This has already been mentioned in the House by the last speaker, I think. The word "trustee" is stricken out. What right have we as the parliament to strike out our obligation as trustees for these people? That obligation was created when this country was formed. What is a trustee? It is a person whom you can trust to protect your interests, and no trustee has any right to say he will not carry on with his obligations any further. If the subject matter of his trust has disappeared, that is another matter, but here it has not. It is still there, and the trusteeship obligation has in fact been substantially ignored.
I am tempted to read to the House some of the provisions of this agreement which we are being asked to approve. I presume that the committee to which this will be referred will have an extremely difficult job. Certainly I do not envy them their job. It was said by Mr. Ciaccia as the representative of Mr. Bourassa, in introducing this agreement:
Every aspect of the agreement must be studied in detail before it becomes law.
Can we say in the House that we will have studied every detail of this agreement before it becomes law? The answer is no. We are just going to approve it in bulk and say that that is all we have to do, all the responsibility we have in this matter.
James Bay Agreement
I do not know when this history is going to end. The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development says that these people approved the agreement. Has he made any effort to discover the circumstances under which they approved, whether they understood it or not? Has he read the history of these agreements in the past whereby Indians and other native peoples were required to give up their rights, their titles and their privileges, their immemorial rights, one might say? They were asked to give them up, and in return they got pieces of paper. Has he thought of that history? I think he cannot have thought of it. Perhaps he has come to this matter at a stage when very little can be done about it. That is so typical of what happens in the House.
The very first project that I had anything to do with in the House was the Columbia River Treaty which General Mac-Naughton and others thought was a give-away of Canada's resources. But it was agreed to by the Governments of Canada, the two governments one after the other. Then we were told in the House and in the committee which studied it, "you can look at this, we do not object to you talking about it, you can call witnesses, but not one comma will be changed". At present we are not quite as crude as that, but the same effect will be achieved. Therefore I ask this House to look at this again and to reject this agreement, at least until it has received the study that it deserves and needs.
