speakeroldname: Mr. Jim Fleming (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, some days ago in this very important debate a member of the opposition, the hon member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Wenman), spent some time talking about environmental concerns as they relate to this bill. I would like, therefore, to spend a few moments tonight answering some of those concerns and, if I may, as well do justice to the minister with whom I work and who, I believe, is absolutely devoted not only to the fisheries side of his portfolio but the environmental side as well.
I take personal exception to the comments of the hon. member for Fraser Valley West, made on December 8, as reported at page 1787 of Hansard, when he said:
Will the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) take a stand for the environment, or will that same minister, who has been given the responsibility for the environment, literally decimate his own department by reallocating his environment budget to sovereignty patrols for the 200 mile limit? I doubt if he will stand and defend the environment of this 68,285 square miles of Canada.
That rather disappoints me because I believe the House of Commons function on the basic thesis that from all sides of the House people will responsibly criticize and propose ideas which are in the interests of the Canadian people. There is no area more important to the immediate future of Canadians than issues of the environment, and there is no issue which will focus more centrally on environmental questions than this James Bay development project. For that reason I am disappointed that the hon. member for Fraser Valley West, who has expressed concerns about environmental aspects and who sometimes addressed himself positively in his speech to the problem, could say that the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment was literally decimating his own department.
Publicly, and at the Standing Committee on Fisheries and Forestry only a week or two earlier, the minister clearly said in response to the official critic for the opposition on environmental issues, and I quote from page 1:30 of the committee report dated November 23, 1976, as follows:
Mr. Chairman, unless I resort to my other official language, I do not think I can match the hon. member's eloquence and use of strong words. 1 would like to make it very clear that if what he called the rape of the environmental services took place, it was also shared in by the other branch of the department, the fisheries and marine service, which in fact absorbed $1.6 million of the additional cost; and the sacrifice, if "sacrifice" is the word we should use, was certainly equally shared.
A few moments later in addressing himself to this earlier charge by the official opposition critic on the environment, the minister said:
I also want to make one other thing clear: no section of a department owns itself. There are periods during which, in any department of government, one segment will have to move into second place in relation to another one. I can visualize the day when, for example, environmental protection services in the

area of environment and energy is going to occupy a very large place in the Department of the Environment. Now, that does not mean that atmospheric services or management services are not important; it simply means that at that point in time the priorities have to be established, and they can only be established by the one or two persons who are above the sections of a department, that is, the deputy minister and the minister.
What I want to argue in beginning my response to the hon. member for Fraser Valley West, and I hope adding some comment on behalf of my minister and his very respected department and public servants in that section federally, is that nothing could be more unfair than to accuse the minister of decimating the environmental section of his department. First of all, the minister in question did not hold the portfolio of minister responsible for the environment last March when the decision was made to give priority within the Departments of Fisheries and the Environment to the issue of adequately coping with the problem of the extension of the fisheries zone for Canada to 200 miles. It was September when the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment (Mr. LeBlanc) became responsible for both areas.
I should say, Mr. Speaker, that in these days of restraint it is very frustrating for someone on the government side to find the opposition so ready, piece by piece, section by section, to demand, with piousness and righteousness, more money and more responsibility when from the other side of their mouths they continue to demand government restraint. I believe that the people of Canada are seriously concerned about government restraint; I also believe it is a real responsibility and challenge for any Government of Canada today to meet those demands and restraints, to show visibly that we are restraining ourselves and, in turn, to meet important priorities. Surely there could be no more important, long range responsibility for the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment than to cope adequately with the challenge of taking care of our responsibilities with an extended 200 miles zone for the fisheries.
As the minister said himself in committee, and as I quoted him a few moments ago, priorities do change from time to time. Yet the charge that one area of his responsibility is decimated, when he was not even minister at the time that decision was taken, and when in turn he has shown in committee and in the House a real concern not only for fisheries, which reflects upon thousands of jobs in an area of depression with high unemployment, and reflects upon a food resource not only essential to Canadians but to the world, seems to me dreadfully unfair when he has also shown this real interest and sensitivity to questions of the environment.
The extension of jurisdiction to the 200 mile limit for Fisheries is of course very important and very much a priority of this department today. I have every reason to believe, and so does the minister and members on this side of the House, that in time, and perhaps not very far ahead, the question of the Environmental Contaminants Act effectively carrying out its responsibility will be very real indeed. At that point we may find that the Minister of Fisheries and the Environment will be redirecting funds under restraint in that direction. To say that any minister cannot reassess priorities within his own department, or having had thrust upon him a new and major
December 14, 1976

responsibility while we have a restraint program, cannot look within and readjust, is to deny the sensitivity that surely the official opposition demands of the government on a daily basis.
The extension of jurisdiction to 200 miles, the current major priority of the Department of Fisheries and the Environment, does not for the moment obliterate the ongoing responsibility not only of the minister but of the government to continue to give a high priority to all environmental matters. When you talk about fisheries and when you talk about the environment, you are, of course, very much talking about one and the same thing. If we talk about jobs, preserving our fishery supply, preserving a key food commodity, developing it at a time when we need more employment and more exports of goods, about the provision of a food commodity to other nations, we cannot discuss those things without also realising that environmental considerations, the health and state of our waters, the supply of our fisheries, are matters that could not make any group more aware of environmental concerns that the people involved in the fisheries industry.
So, Mr. Speaker, next month or next year the concern may well be energy and environmental concern-pipelines and environmental concern-or in fact this James Bay bill we are talking about tonight, and environmental concerns. Surely a minister must have the freedom to skim, be rigid and tough where he can, and focus where he must in order to carry out government responsibilities.
For a few moments I should like to dwell on particular criticisms made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley West. From listening to previous speakers you get the impression in this debate that the role of Environment Canada in the James Bay project is not clearly understood. I should like to spend a few moments trying to make it better understood.
The role of the Department of Fisheries and the Environment should be viewed in its proper context. The James Bay project is a Quebec project, being constructed by a provincial Crown corporation, financed by the province and, from the physical point of view, impacts will be largely on matters under provincial jurisdiction.
While the announcement by the former premier, Mr. Bou-rassa, in 1971 indicated that a hydro-electric project would be built in the James Bay area, the exact location was not specified at that time. Therein lay a role of major importance for the federal department at that time. Shortly after that announcement the province of Quebec asked the department to take part in a task force to determine, among other things, which alternative being considered-the La Grande or Notta-way-Broadback Report (NBR)-would be most acceptable environmentally.
With limited data, and after about two months of investigation, the task force concluded that the La Grande alternative would appear to be less demaging to the environment than the NBR. That was a major thrust and a major role played by Environment Canada.
It is interesting to note that even in 1971, five long years ago and before we arrived at this point, the task force report
James Bay Agreement
emphasized that the major impact of the development would be on the native population and not the physical environment. As far as I am aware, this was the first report to highlight the consequences to the natives-again an action by Environment Canada which played an important role of influence in this developing situation.
Shortly after the report was published early in 1972 the government of Quebec announced its intention to proceed with the La Grande development-the recommendation of Environment Canada. In June, 1972, Environment Canada officers met with officials of the James Bay development corporation to outline a program of environmental studies necessary to determine the potential impact of the project.
In November, 1972, Quebec and Canada signed an agreement to enable the necessary environmental studies to be carried out in the James Bay region. It covered the period 1971 to 1975 inclusive, and included studies already under way. Again, Mr. Speaker, this was a major role and thrust of Environment Canada. While the total program was outlined, Environment Canada accepted responsibility for the cost of studies within its jurisdiction, the province for its exclusive responsibilities, and programs of mutual interest were cost-shared on a 50-50 basis. The program was co-ordinated by a federal-provincial steering committee. So before we accept as rote the comments of the hon. member for Fraser Valley West, I should like to make it clear that where Environment Canada and the government had the power, we made a major thrust in choosing the location and paying our way, and thus involving ourselves in environmental recommendations.
To carry out its responsibilities under the four-year agreement, Environment Canada committed itself to an expenditure of $6 million and to further cost-share studies in the amount of $4 million. Surely that is visible evidence that the federal government, in this period of restraint, was concerned about how native peoples would be treated and about the choice of proper locations. The department, acting under the authority of the federal government, spent money and took concrete action to bring about the most reasonable solution.
In the fall of 1972 the Indians and Inuit sought an interim injunction to halt the James Bay project. That action was significant in the development of this situation. Environment Canada made its information and experts available to all parties to the injunction. Without bias or prejudice the federal government through Environment Canada said to the Inuit and other natives, and to the government of Quebec, "Here are our facts and figures. We want to influence you because we want you to recognize the environmental problems we see."
During the court proceedings presided over by Judge Malouf, Environment Canada officials appeared voluntarily as witnesses both for the natives and the province. Between November, 1973, and November, 1974, department officials had some involvement in the agreement in principle. Unfortunately, and I say this personally, because of the split in our constitutional powers federally and provincially, limitations

December 14, 1976
James Bay Agreement
were placed on the ability of Environment Canada to be involved more directly in the issue.
Based on the information to date from their environmental studies, Environment Canada scientists prepared in 1974, and published early in 1975, a report outlining, to the extent possible, the environmental concerns arising from the proposed development. Again, further information was made available to the natives and to the developers. In that report not only were environmental impacts identified, but areas in which there would be little or no impact were outlined. In addition certain recommendations for remedial measures were specified. Acting within its jurisdiction, Environment Canada clearly carried out its mandate and clearly gave advice and direction. It is fair to say that, whether or not their recommendations were all accepted, all major parties to the agreement, including the natives, were made aware of them.
It can also be stated that most of the provisions for environmental protection and remedial measures built into the agreement were as a result of the constant participation of Environment Canada officials. To ensure a continuation of the environmental studies in the James Bay region, Environment Canada renewed the federal-provincial agreement to the end of March, 1979. Total cost of the program will be $2.25 million, to be cost shared on a 50-50 basis.
Finally, Environment Canada feels that, if the provisions contained in sections 22 and 23 of the agreement are implemented, the natives will be afforded the opportunity to participate in a fashion without precedence in the management of the environment in the James Bay region.
May I sum up, Mr. Speaker, and allow others to participate in this debate. The federal Department of Fisheries and the Environment without question by its efforts influenced the outcome of the negotiations. That input resulted in certain changes to original design. It resulted in provision for remedial works as part of an agreement with natives. That input from Environment Canada also resulted in the formulation of structures to ensure that all future development is reviewed by appropriate committees, including representation by natives and Department of Fisheries and the Environment officials.
Although hon. members of this House from time to time are partisan, angry and frustrated, it is essential for all members, in carrying out their responsibilities, to deal with issues about which they have some expertise. In this case, although the hon. member for Fraser Valley West made some positive points in his speech, I was a little disappointed that he should so personally and directly attack the minister, a minister who has such respect for members on the hon. member's side of the House. The minister has done important work in finding employment, protecting our fisheries and expanding our jurisdiction to the 200-mile limit. That minister, who is weighed down with all that responsibility, has demonstrated in committee and in the House that he cares about the environment, is willing to represent all Canadians and act, within the restraint guidelines, both to uphold the priorities of the government and demonstrate that the federal government is most concerned about the sensitive area of the environment.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to express some of my views on the subject being debated.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext: Briefly, I hope.

subtopic: JAMES BAY AND NORTHERN QUEBEC NATIVE CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO GIVE EFFECT TO AGREEMENTS WITH NATIVES OF NORTHERN QUEBEC
speechtext:
Yes, I shall be brief, for the benefit of those who want to go home early. I thought it might be useful to review some of the history of this matter. We know that the present Liberal government in Ottawa has not done much to recognize and protect Indian rights. Indeed that has been the history of the Liberal party in dealings with the Indians right from the beginning. We know, for example, that the Conservative party was the first political party in this House officially to recognize some years ago the existence of aboriginal rights. The other parties followed suit some time later.
Under previous Liberal administrations the native peoples of this country were not allowed to vote. The Progressive Conservative government led by the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) gave the native peoples, particularly treaty Indians, the right to vote. According to my interpretation, that was the first genuine step any government had taken to involve the Indian peoples in the mainstream of Canadian life, in which I include participation in the political process. As I recall, at that time old age pensions were first extended to the Indian peoples, something which had not been done by governments previous to the Conservative government to which I referred.
The particular agreement we are debating has met with mixed reaction on the part of our native peoples. I am sure I am right in saying that, since I shall soon quote excerpts from documents expressing their views and supporting my contention. Chief Billy Diamond of the Cree Grand Council described the agreement as "the best settlement made with Indian peoples in North America." His enthusiasm was not shared by the Indians of Quebec Association. Chief Andrew Delisle expressed grave reservations about the agreement. Allow me to quote the last paragraph of the letter Chief Delisle sent to my colleague, the hon. member for Lambton-Kent (Mr. Holmes), which reads as follows:
The governments may have threatened the Cree and the Inuit of James Bay that if they did not sign, they would get nothing; but they would still have their aboriginal rights, whatever they may feel them to be as well as their right to claim in the future; and the government would have been forced by moral and legal obligation to provide for them. As it stands, the government took the lands and the rights anyway. But I doubt whether they could have forced the Cree to become Quebecers who are fighting for special status because the Cree already had special status which they lost when they signed the agreement, only to get it partially returned in the agreement.
Although the Quebec Indian Association expressed reservations, to be fair we must commend the Cree Grand Council for arriving at an agreement which was an historical landmark, if nothing else. Negotiating in difficult conditions, they arrived at an agreement which was satisfactory to a substantial number of people directly affected. There was concern in case this agreement became a precedent or pattern for future agreements in other areas in which there are a good number of unsettled Indian claims. I am thinking of the Inuit claim which had been made to the Arctic Archipelago, the Northwest
December 14, 1976

Territories claim submitted in the Dene proposals, and other non-status Indian claims in the Northwest Territories, the Yukon, British Columbia and, indeed, even in my constituency in northeast Alberta.
There are claims all over this country which are far from settled. I will outline them. There was a treaty involving an Indian band located at Fort Chipewyan in 1918 or 1920. Part of the agreement was that they should be given some land of their choice. They still do not have it. They are still waiting for land which the federal government agreed to give back in 1920.
The government should bring forward legislation very soon to allocate a portion of Wood Buffalo Park which these people have chosen to satisfy this unfulfilled land entitlement in that area. It is three years since the Fort Chipewyan Crees came to an agreement with the federal government on the site and size of the new reserve in Wood Buffalo Park. However, for some strange reason legislation has not been forthcoming from this government.
Another claim has been laid to a substantial portion of the tar sands in northern Alberta by the Alberta Indian Association. In view of the importance of the tar sands to Canadian energy supplies, the government should begin talks with the native people in that area to try to come to some kind of agreement in so far as land claims are concerned. Working out some kind of settlement before a great deal of development has taken place would avoid very substantial problems that could arise in the future.
I want to make it clear that neither I nor my party are trying to be paternalistic in this debate by expressing reservations about an agreement arrived at through negotiation between Indian people, governments and other bodies, particularly since the negotiators from the Indian side appear to be satisfied in some ways, at least. However, I have to say that under the system by which this institution operates, namely, the adversary system, we have an obligation to parliament to point out the other side of the coin. Members on the government side would never do that. They always have a tendency to cover up possible difficulties that could occur as a result of their proposals. I am sure Your Honour can think of many examples of that.
We as a party are very concerned that any such proposal being debated in this House must be looked at very carefully and thoroughly from all sides. It is the job of the official opposition, indeed of all members of parliament, to ensure that all of the facts are laid on the table before a vote is taken.
I found it rather curious when the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Allmand) spoke. He talked about the settlement as an agreement covering that area as referred to in the legislation. He said:
The area covered by the proposed legislation comprises 410,000 square miles, or about 60 per cent of the province of Quebec-
I checked the minister's calculations. I found that 410,000 square miles actually amounts to roughly 70 per cent of what
James Bay Agreement
is presently known as the area belonging to the province of Quebec. By strange coincidence, it works out to about 60 per cent if you combine Labrador and Quebec. I don't know whether the minister in his proposal was putting forward a proposal on behalf of his new Quebec provincial government or not. Perhaps he owes this House an explanation to clarify how he arrived at these calculations and why, particularly when the government and citizens of Newfoundland would not take too kindly to that kind of consideration.
I am a little concerned about that part of the agreement which seems to turn over a responsibility which the laws of Canada give to the federal government. In this agreement the federal government is to a certain extent turning over its responsibility to the provincial government of Quebec, particularly with regard to health and social services. The Indian people should be very cautious in accepting this kind of proposal, particularly in view of the current level of instability in so far as the political situation in the province of Quebec is concerned.
Referring to the Indian Association of Quebec previously, I stated they had some very grave reservations about this agreement. I suppose the reasons for those reservations could be summarized in one sentence. Basically the native people have agreed to renounce all further land claims against the government in exchange for the benefits of this agreement.
The agreement contains several clauses. One deals with a $225 million tax free cash payment to the native people. It also deals with a land settlement, the land being divided into three categories and amounting to a few thousand square miles of territory. The environmental portion of the agreement to which the parliamentary secretary addressed himself raises a question about which I am a little nervous from the point of view of native rights.
Four regulatory bodies have been established to oversee development. On two of the bodies, the Environmental and Social Impact Review Committee and the Environmental and Social Impact Panel, will decide the fate of proposed new developments in areas of provincial or federal jurisdiction. They will be composed of two Cree appointments and three governmental appointees. In essence what we have is the establishment of a body where native people can make representations but they will in fact be the minority. The appropriate government official will make the final decision on development when there is a lack of mutual agreement on such developments.
There is also a provision for the establishment of local governments and the preservation of certain hunting, fishing and trapping rights, and another payment to be made under the economic and social measures clause which reads as follows:
Those who wish to earn a living from harvesting of game will get a guaranteed annual income from Quebec of $2,400 per person maximum.
I am a little concerned about that. We know that in treaties made a long time ago at that time there may have appeared to have been a substantial sum of money, but 100 years later it becomes a very insubstantial sum.
2018

December 14, 1976
James Bay Agreement
We are now looking at $2,400 a year. Projecting that 100 years, and given the current inflation rate, say the average inflation rate of the past ten years which was around 5.6 per cent, $2,400 a year will amount to the equivalent of about $12 a year.
If we look at it in those terms, which we must do when dealing with agreements that are supposed to be in perpetuity, we have to look ahead 100 or 200 years or even more, because the definition of "in perpetuity" is forever. In 100 years from now, $12 a year will not go very far in terms of helping to support an Indian family. That is another area that should be reviewed. Perhaps some kind of an indexing formula should be worked out if this clause is to have any meaning whatsoever from the long term point of view.
I wish to put on record a few more quotations from the letter written by the President of the Indians of Quebec Association with reference to what the Indian people have lost through this agreement. The letter says:
We have lost the right to be Indian over all of the land, for we are Indian only on our reserves. We have lost the right to be taught by our parents and elders. We have lost the right to regulate our lives in peace and security and to judge ourselves. We have lost the right to speak our own language. We have lost the right to go into business as Indians.
We have lost many of our ways, not through the process of evolution, but by force. We have lost the right to build shelter for we have lost the animals and the trees; we cannot even build a log cabin without first having to get permission from a lumber or pulp and paper company.
Over the years we have lost mentally and physically many of our people by sickness, alcohol, drugs, bad care, misunderstanding, bad management, prejudice, discrimination, fighting your wars, mistreatment and shame. You count the ways, the time, the dollars.
Chief Delisle briefly outlines the situation which in his view the Indian people are facing. It is a situation common to many areas which are covered by treaties and to some which were not covered by treaties at all.
I should like to continue by quoting the view expressed by James Arvaluk, President of the Inuit Tapirisat. He says: "We are saddened we are giving up so much for so little." So not everyone on the native side is happy about the terms of the agreement. I might add that this agreement is of particular importance inasmuch as it might be considered as a pattern to be followed in the settlement of other claims likely to arise in the course of the next few years. Thus it is vital that the document should be fair to the native people as well as to the other parties involved.
One difficulty appears to be arising already; it relates to the process of land selection. I am informed that talks in this area have already broken down because Quebec wants to involve Hydro Quebec and is using land choice criteria which are not in the agreement. While the general terms of reference are outlined in the agreement itself, land choice may be far more difficult that anyone has predicted. The Quebec Indian Association has asked the federal government to step in to ensure that the Quebec government follows the terms of the agreement. I think this is significant in itself.
[Mr. Yewchuk-1
Charges have been made against the federal government by the native people, particularly in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon, that they were living under colonial status. Charges have been laid by Indian people all over the country that the Indian Act is paternalistic, as is the attitude of the government toward the native people. When we review the developments which have taken place during the last 100 years or so, we find there is a great deal of truth in the assertion. The treaties made with the Indians are based to a great extent on the concept of paternalism, and examining the economic, social and educational development which has taken place since treaties of this kind were entered into, we can readily see that development of Indian people has not been very satisfactory.
In order to emphasize the importance of ensuring that agreements are properly made, I think I should make reference to Treaty No. 6. This is not to say that the agreement we are discussing can be classified as a treaty. But I believe we can still learn something from Treaty No. 6-this was the treaty made between the Cree Indian people, the Woodland and Plains Cree tribe of Northern Alberta and Saskatchewan, where they ceded most of their land and were placed on reserves. The terms of that treaty were as follows:
The Plain and Wood Cree tribes of Indians and all other Indians inhabiting the district hereinafter described and defined, do hereby cede, release, surrender and yield up to the government of the Dominion of Canada, for Her Majesty the Queen and Her successors forever, all their rights, titles and privileges whatsoever to the lands included within the following limits-
The treaty then goes on to describe the areas ceded. It is clear that the Indians were giving up the very means of livelihood they had enjoyed for hundreds of years. In return, they were placed on reserves, one square mile being allotted to each family of five, or each portion thereof. There was also a grant of $12 to each man, woman and child belonging to the bands, and in addition each band was given $1,500 a year for the purchase of ammunition and twine for nets. Further, they were given various agricultural implements with the idea that the Indian people, after being hunters and fishermen for generations, would suddenly become farmers. We all recognize now that this notion did not materialize.
Another thing which struck me as I reviewed this treaty was that special concessions were made to the chiefs and head men. Each chief received an annual salary in addition to the payment made to members of the rest of the band, and each subordinate officer was guaranteed an annual salary amounting to $25. I have taken the trouble to interpret that figure in terms of the worth of the dollar today. It appears the difference is not as great as one might have thought, because $25 then had about the same purchasing power as $100 today. The chiefs were also given a wagon and some horses, a set of clothing, a flag, a medal, and a number of other items which were not made available to the rest of the Indian population. It seems to me that if one wanted to be suspicious one could conclude there was an element of bribery involved. I hope that in future negotiations with native people special privileges and concessions of this kind will not be offered to the negotiators themselves, because when circumstances of that kind become
December 14, 1976

evident one is apt to wonder whether the negotiators worked as hard as they could to secure the best deal for those they represented.
I have already referred to the need, when negotiating monetary settlements which are to be in effect in perpetuity, to remember the inflation factor. Most people when they talk of long-term contracts have a period of 10, 15, perhaps 20 years in mind. If there are to be settlements made that will offer certain payments to the Indian people on an annual basis, it would be worth remembering that if we have $1,000 today, with an annual inflation rate of 7 per cent that $1,000 will only be worth $1.15 in one hundred years.
If we consider the present value of $1 million, two hundred years down the road that will only be worth $1.32 with a 7 per cent inflation rate. In considering these kind of figures we might think of a $5,000 car today which in 100 years would cost $1 million. When we talk about a settlement of $1 million it sounds like a lot of money today, but 100 years down the road it does not amount to very much. Let us consider a $10,000 car, which is not unusual at today's prices. With a 7 per cent annual inflation rate that car would cost $2 million one hundred years from now. If we take it another step, one hundred years from now we might end up paying $40 for a chocolate bar.
All these factors should be considered very carefully when we are talking about a financial agreement which will entitle the native people to certain payments on an annual basis. In order to keep everything in perspective, when this kind of agreement is made the native people should strive to have an indexing factor built in to take care of the inflationary problems which we are far from solving at the moment.
With those remarks I will conclude. There are others in this Chamber who are waiting for the vote and are anxious to get home to watch television. That probably is more fun than listening to me speak.

subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF DISTRICT OFFICES-REQUEST FOR OFFICE AT BRANDON, MANITOBA
VETERANS AFFAIRS-PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF DISTRICT OFFICES-REQUEST FOR OFFICE AT BRANDON, MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 19 I directed a question to the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. MacDonald) with respect to the plan to decentralize the services of the Department of Veterans Affairs. The specific question dealt with the advisability of having a service officer in the city of Brandon to meet the needs of the large population of service men living in the western Manitoba area.
The minister indicated at that time that the matter was under consideration. In a supplementary question I inquired if he was aware that not only was there not a resident service officer for this important part of the province of Manitoba but that for the past few months it has been impossible to receive or make long distance telephone calls to the Department of Veterans Affairs in Winnipeg, which means that these veterans are without adequate service.
I know that the department is in the process of decentralization on a massive scale which, over a period of six years, will remove the headquarters from Ottawa to Charlottetown in Prince Edward Island. It seems to me, however, in the light of what has been happening in the downgrading of services to our veterans' population, that it is more a phasing out of services than a decentralization of services. This is the point I should like to make this evening, Mr. Speaker. The government has been downgrading the military service and it would appear the same process is under way with respect to the services provided for the veterans of Canada.
Mr. Bob Adams, who is the director general of veterans services, has indicated in an article in the Canadian Legion for October, 1976, that there is a plan afoot to increase the number of district officers in the area where the clients are-a storefront operation with as little support as possible. This is precisely the sort of service I am recommending and I trust whoever replies for the minister tonight will give a positive response and indicate that this is the plan for serving western Manitoba.
Part of the phasing out of services for veterans has included a decrease in travel. In Manitoba in the past several months it has been almost impossible to have the direct assistance of a service officer unless the matter was one of dire emergency. I would say that if this is the case it is all the more reason why long distance telephoning should be available. In his article Mr. Adams indicated that long distance telephoning was going to be substituted for direct travel arrangements.
I have been corresponding with the minister for over a year on this problem, Mr. Speaker, so he is aware of it. In a letter to me dated April 6, he wrote:
December 14, 1976

Thank you for writing to me about the possibility of establishing a full time departmental representative in Brandon to serve the Westman area. I assure you that this matter, and the excellent material which accompanied your letter, will receive careful and thorough review.
We are not putting forward a new proposition, Mr. Speaker. This has been under consideration for a year, and I trust that the minister or his representative will give a positive response tonight. The Canadian Legion has been trying to fill the gap by stepping up its service operation to veterans, but as Mr. Adams said in the article, some Legion service officers are just not sufficiently familiar with the appropriate legislation. The Legion has done magnificent service, but I suggest that DVA still has the prime responsibility and it would meet a real need if it provided a service officer in the Westman area.

speakeroldname: Mr. S. Victor Railton (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: VETERANS AFFAIRS-PROPOSED ESTABLISHMENT OF DISTRICT OFFICES-REQUEST FOR OFFICE AT BRANDON, MANITOBA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to reply to the question raised by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale), who I know is greatly concerned about this matter. He has corresponded with the department and the minister for some time. His interest goes back some years; it is an interest which the hon. member has expressed in the veterans affairs committee.
The hon. member is concerned about the phasing out of certain services. I feel that, rather than being phased out, some of the services of the Veterans Affairs department are likely to increase in volume. Therefore I think I can lay his mind to rest on that point.
The hon. member is concerned about the effects of decentralization. It has been established that during the next three of four years, when the actual move from Ottawa may take place, the decentralization of the department will have no deleterious effects on service to veterans. Actually such service may be enhanced because of the improved communications system which will be in use.
From the standpoint of the Royal Canadian Legion, Operation Service is a good idea about which we are enthusiastic, because it has brought to light cases of veterans who otherwise would not have been aware of the benefits the Government of Canada was making available to them. A great many veterans have been completely ignorant of what they should have been receiving. I congratulate the Royal Canadian Legion on the great work they have done this year through Operation Service.
If the minister were here this evening I know he would say that the officials of the department have been examining the field organizational structure, paying particular attention to service outlets in relation to client population density and related costs. This study is primarily concerned with providing easier access to departmental services for veterans and their dependants. However, it is also seeking more efficiency in operations during a period of restraint. One of the ideas which can serve both these purposes is the adoption of store front-types of operations, to which my hon. friend has referred.
Adjournment Debate
It is too early in the study to be specific as to exact locations of service outlets, but I can assure you that the Brandon, Manitoba, area is under serious consideration. Also, I should like to thank the hon. member for his helpful suggestions made in correspondence to the minister earlier this year.
With respect to the matter of long distance telephone calls to veterans outside the greater Winnipeg area, officials of DVA assure us that no such restrictions exist, nor in their recollection have there ever been such restrictions. In fact the staff of the district director of veterans services in Winnipeg make extensive use of the telephone in speeding up service to veterans, particularly those located in remote areas.
I therefore feel that the well expressed worry and concern of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris have been answered by the document which has been prepared for the minister. I assure him that both the minister and the department will do everything in their power to make sure that the hon. member's cause for worry is removed.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-POSSIBLE SHORTAGE OF REFRIGERATED CARS FOR MOVEMENT OF POTATOES-SUGGESTED PURCHASE OF ADDITIONAL CARS
TRANSPORT-POSSIBLE SHORTAGE OF REFRIGERATED CARS FOR MOVEMENT OF POTATOES-SUGGESTED PURCHASE OF ADDITIONAL CARS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 30 last I questioned the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) about the possible-if not probable-shortage of temperature-controlled boxcars for the transport of Maritime potatoes this winter and in the immediate future. In response the minister said that he foresaw no problem this winter, but could not comment satisfactorily with respect to a longer term solution. Indeed with respect to this winter the minister suggested, and I quote, "The basic view is there should be adequate equipment and the Canadian National is looking to see if that is the case." That is less than a satisfactory answer, Mr. Speaker, in light of the rapid deterioration in the number and quality of reefer cars presently available.
I raise the matter tonight again because the minister's answer did not properly reflect the urgency of the situation, a misunderstanding at least which must be cleared up if there is to be any rational discussion and action. Markets in central Canada are crucial outlets for the maritime potato crop. Over 85 per cent of our potatoes now move to Toronto and Montreal markets by temperature-controlled cars.
Six to ten years ago there were 4,000 reefer cars in service. Today, at most 1,500 are available, and as many as 500, one third of these, will be withdrawn from service within the year. Incredibly, all are rented from an American company which finds their dilapidated state just too costly to keep in repair. In fact there are strong indications that the company wishes to abandon the whole fleet as soon as possible. This would be a catastrophe.
CN has persuaded itself, and I presume the minister too, that a very rapid transition can take place from complete rail to a mixed rail and highway transportation system for the potato bulk traffic, although the problem could be brought to crisis proportions this winter in view of the high level of

December 14, 1976
Adjournment Debate
overseas export shipment of potatoes contracted for this year. Prince Edward Island ports are virtually closed for the winter, necessitating the use of Halifax and Saint John. Compared to the normal 150 reefer cars needed for this market, an estimated 500 cars will be required this year. Clearly the system is approaching the overload point, and assurances to the contrary rest on the very dubious assumption that the rail car turnaround time can be rapidly and drastically improved, inasmuch as on an average basis some 8,000 car trips are required in Prince Edward Island alone during the shipping season.
The pressure on the decreasing number of reefer cars is alarming, to say the least. When I questioned the minister, he said he was not yet quite sure what mode of transport was most appropriate. At the end of his answer, the minister said, and I quote:
Therefore, the mode of transportation which should be used need not necessarily be refrigerated cars.
So far the minister has not stated what form or alternate form will be acceptable. He implied that rail transport was not necessarily essential to transporting the potato crop off Prince Edward Island, that highway trailers might be able to do the job. This sounds like the CN management talking. They are obviously living in some kind of a dream world, for two reasons at least. First, the present Prince Edward Island highways system is not up to the job. It has been estimated that anywhere between $10 million and $20 million will have to be spent immediately, and obviously the minister has not tried to drive on island roads during spring thaw, a time when between one quarter and one third of our crop is in fact shipped out.
In addition, in terms of vehicles available to move the amount of potatoes, this too is extremely wishful thinking. It has not even been decided who would purchase and who would own these particular trailers. CN management has also suggested that it would be an additional cost to the system to purchase new railroad cars. I find this passing strange, as I do not think that in the case of hopper cars for grain in western Canada those costs are attributable to producers.
Apart from the fact 90 per cent of P.E.I.'s potato warehouses are not properly equipped to handle trucks, which would force costly alterations on island shippers, the expense of upgrading and maintaining island roads for all-weather use would be phenomenal, and of course CN might prefer not to keep the railbeds in condition and let the province pay for highways, but obviously P.E.I. does not have that kind of money available. One is inclined to agree with the recent meeting of the Maritime premiers who stated, and I quote:
There is an alarming lack of hard evidence that transportation is being used as a positive development tool.
The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has recognized the grave needs that exist, and in comments both in New Brunswick and to journalists here, has indicated that he is preparing a memo to cabinet urging that 1,000 reefer cars be ordered immediately. I trust that he has already made active representation to the Minister of Transport. What are needed as a minimum, and the minister can check with the P.E.I. Potato Marketing Board if he doubts my figures, are 800

heated, insulated boxcars of about 50-ton capacity, phased in over a five-year period. These would give our rail system added flexibility in all regions, and I have not yet mentioned the uses these cars would have in permitting more efficient two-way usage between the maritimes and central Canada.
One final point, reefer boxcars offer the government the opportunity to provide a creative and integrated response to regional disparity. The minister met with representatives of the Hawker Siddeley plant in Trenton yesterday. He indicated that the government was on the verge of making a decision with respect to an order for grain cars to offset an unemployment crisis there. Obviously the same sort of decision with respect to insulated boxcars would be a tremendous boost to industrial activity in the Pictou County area of Nova Scotia, and would also establish a much firmer transportation mode for one of our basic commodities in Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, that of potatoes.

subtopic: AGRICULTURE-BEEF-POSSIBILITY OF PROHIBITING IMPORTS FROM AUSTRALIA AND NEW ZEALAND
AGRICULTURE-BEEF-POSSIBILITY OF PROHIBITING IMPORTS FROM AUSTRALIA AND NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take up this evening a question which I put to the minister yesterday. I do so because I believe the answer which I received is confusing the agricultural industry and, in particular, those engaged in the marketing of beef.
The minister has once again hidden behind the veil of the GATT agreement with the Oceanic countries, indicating thereby that nothing can be done about the depressed state of beef markets in Canada. As the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Pelletier) knows, ranchers and farmers in this country are entering upon their fourth year of producing below the cost of production. The situation is a
December 14, 1976

very serious one, and a great many farmers and ranchers across the prairies are going bankrupt. In my own constituency, at least 17 large ranchers will be forced to sell out this year because of the devastating situation to which I have referred.
It is my hope that the parliamentary secretary will give us tonight what one might call an operational definition of what the department considers to be supply management. This is important, because there is a great deal of trepidation across the country arising from the use of the term "supply management". The concept is scarcely working in the case of the poultry industry, one in which essentially you buy a hen a year which lays, theoretically, an egg a day. That is the kind of situation which supply and management ought to be able to cover, but when one gets into the beef industry one is looking at a five-year cycle from the time the calves are born to the time the product is finally sold. In terms of such an operation the phrase "supply management" is a very dubious one as it affects quotas and controls. Yet the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) in response to the question claimed that the United States has a supply-management system simply on the basis that it has quotas against Oceanic countries.
I tabled in the House of Commons this day a petition with in excess of 5,000 names. Those names were collected by a citizens' group with virtually no effort at all. All of them are saying emphatically that one thing they do not want is a supply-management system. I know full well that if the minister means that we cut off quotas from Oceanic countries, and he calls that supply-management, indeed that is exactly what we are after. What we are not after is a situation in which there are quotas put on the ranchers and they are dictated to by the government as to how to run the business in the farmyard.
Unfortunately the situation is that there has not been a definition and people are extremely confused about that which we are calling supply-management. On October 29, in response to a comment I made earlier that day, the minister stated, as reported at page 605 of Hansard:
The hon. member for Battle River is circulating a petition against the supply-management of beef. Let me tell him that 1 cannot do it to the farmers of Canada unless they want it, because it is not in the legislation. He is using scare tactics.
Let me simply suggest that one of the things the minister cannot escape is the fact that he is the Minister of Agriculture and has an obligation to the agricultural industry.
Let me ask the parliamentary secretary through you, Mr. Speaker, how it is that a basically western cultured industry that is so important to the three prairie provinces and British Columbia is unable to get the kind of protection it needs through import quotas, when in fact the textile industry in this country suffered for only a short period of time, certainly a period of only a few months, when the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Chretien) saw fit on November 29 to introduce in this House a statement and subsequent regulation to place import quotas on textiles, providing a basic protection for the central Canada market?
Adjournment Debate
I have no argument with the fact that the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce should do what is within his jurisdiction to protect Canadians, but I think it is a complete fallacy to claim on the one hand that the United States is acting illegally in terms of its agreement with GATT, while allowing Canada at a time of domestice over-supply to import the highest amount of beef ever imported into this country under the guise of making the Anti-Inflation Board look like it is working, and giving central Canada what they would assume to be a short-term cheap food policy. The fact of the matter is that in due course the consumer markets in the larger cities in central Canada will have to pay more because we will be losing the beef industry in this country, and this is evidenced by the fact that the number of heifers and cows being sent to market is at an unprecedented rate because the people are being forced out of business through the minister's failure to give protection to the industry.
What we will find in fact then is that while there may be the appearance of a short-term gain, making it look like the anti-inflation program is working, in the long-term food prices will be higher. There has been a deliberate and malicious attempt on behalf of various members of Cabinet, through the Department of Industry, Trade and others, to import many foods into this country, and I would cite honey, fruits, vegetables, pork, poultry and beef as examples, to an extent never before seen in this country so as to give the illusion that we are in fact experiencing a successful anti-inflation program.
I documented this in a speech earlier in November, Mr. Speaker, when I went through the actual import increases which had taken place in this country, showing that in virtually every one of these cases we were in excess of 100 per cent over imports of one year ago, and in some instances over 300 per cent.
With regard to beef marketing, the increase of imports from New Zealand has been 139 per cent, and there has also been an increase of imports from Australia to the point where 90 million pounds of beef are now entering this country. The Minister of Agriculture has to accept his obligation and offer some protection to the industry, and certainly he should be able to follow the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and give the same kind of protection to the western provinces which has been given to the central Canadian textile industry. There also needs to be an operational definition which tells us what in fact-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AGRICULTURE-BEEF-POSSIBILITY OF PROHIBITING IMPORTS FROM AUSTRALIA AND NEW ZEALAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the parliamentary secretary, who is on official duty with regard to the important conference of ministers of agriculture from across the country, I should point out that I do not have time to answer all the points raised by the hon. member. However, one point raised by the hon. member reflects the minister's point of view and

Adjournment Debate
the department's point of view. The minister said that in Canada there can be found cheap food. I think that is quite right because although the Anti-Inflation Board has no jurisdiction over agricultural producers, it has control over processors and control to the point where food reaches the tables of consumers.
On December 13 the hon. member asked for a projection for early 1977 and whether there is an anticipated full cut off of quotas with regard to Oceanic beef.
No decisions have been made regarding the Canadian import regime for 1977. Obviously 1976 has been a difficult year for the Canadian beef industry, with imports at an unprecedented level. There have also been unusually high numbers of cow slaughterings both in beef and dairy herds. At the same time feed costs and other costs have been higher, with the result that beef farmers have been particularly hard hit. However, problems arising from the domestic situation will have to be addressed on their own merits.
The main determinant of the import situation will be whether Canada is faced with constraints on its shipments of beef and veal to the U.S. market. If this is so, constraints on imports into the Canadian market will be necessary to avoid further distortions in the market situation.
Consultations with the United States on this matter are currently under way and will be followed, as necessary, by consultations with our other trading partners in order to arrive at a solution in keeping with our obligations to Australia and New Zealand as members of both the Commonwealth and GATT, as the minister pointed out earlier, and a solution which meets the needs of the beef industry.
I ask hon. members to read the speech delivered by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) at the conference of ministers of agriculture yesterday.
